bio.en: Jen Abel is the co-founder of Jellyfish (JJELLYFISH), where she and her team help early-stage founders learn how to sell, do customer discovery, and build a repeatable sales motion; this episode is an ultra-tactical guide to founder-led sales from zero to one.
bio.zh: Jen Abel 是 Jellyfish（JJELLYFISH）的联合创始人，她和团队帮助早期创始人学习如何销售、做客户探索并建立起可复制的销售动作；这期节目是关于从 0 到 1 的“创始人式销售”的极致实战指南。

summary.en: Jen gets extremely tactical on founder-led sales, treating the founder as the product and the goal as learning as fast as possible rather than revenue on day one. She covers how to craft counterintuitive, shock-value messaging that earns a read, how to structure the first sales call with vulnerability ('I'm early-stage, help me learn'), how to find and reach leads, get through procurement, and close. With actual words, phrases, and pitfalls at every step, it's an episode packed with advice you can put into practice tomorrow—the most hands-on sales conversation you'll find.
summary.zh: Jen 就“创始人式销售”给出极其具体的建议，把创始人本身当作产品，把目标定为“尽可能快地学习”而非第一天就要收入。她讲了如何写出反直觉、有冲击力的信息以赢得一读、如何在第一次销售电话中以坦诚示弱（“我们很早期，请帮我看看这个问题在你们那边是怎么发生的”）、如何找到并触达线索、通过采购流程并签约。每一步都附上真实话术、措辞与坑，这期节目充满了你明天就能用上的建议——是你所能找到最手把手的销售对话。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So if you can focus the messaging in a way that speaks to something that is a bit of shock value or is counterintuitive, you'll get them to continue reading. When a problem is truly being felt by the market, people will get on a call, people will respond.
turns.zh: 因此，如果你能将信息传达得既引人注目又出人意料，就能吸引读者继续阅读。当市场真正感受到某个问题时，人们会参与电话会议，积极响应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The next step I imagine is you're on the phone with them trying to convince them to actually care. What do you do there? How do you get them to engage further?

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You need to be vulnerable. I would be very open and honest with where you are. Hey, I'm an early stage startup. We have a lot to learn. Can we kind of gain your insight into how this problem is manifesting on your side? Founder led sales is not about revenue on day one. It is about learning as fast as humanly possible to get to that pulse, so that you can earn the right to sell.

turns.speaker: Jen Abel

It means that you are a subject matter expert on something highly specific. (00:04:23): You have studied, you have experienced something that most of the market hasn't even had a chance to maybe see or visualize yet. So you have this novel insight that you are building a business around. And it's that novel insight and the way you see the world that gets the market excited, in absence of a product. And that's actually happens even before you even show the product. So founder led sales is how do you bring the founders vision into the world and have the market, and understand what part of the market accepts it, and then what part of that vision are they accepting? So it's aligning the founders vision with the market reality.
turns.zh: 创始人主导的销售实际上是初创公司在商业层面迈出的首个里程碑——即如何走出去，获取首批客户？有人可能会说"从零到一"，即如何实现首笔百万营收；也有人会说"如何争取首批10位客户"，但本质上都是殊途同归。创始人主导的销售至关重要，因为在初创期——当品牌尚未形成、营销引擎尚未启动、客户参考案例寥寥无几之时——创始人本身就是产品。毕竟产品可能还处于抽象阶段，或是仅为最简可行产品（MVP），甚至尚在萌芽期。因此，创始人就是产品。当有人问"这到底意味着什么？"答案是：你要成为某个特定领域的专家。你深入研究、亲身经历了市场中大多数人尚未见识或想象过的事物。你基于这些独到见解构建商业模式。即便产品尚未成型，这种新颖的洞察力与独特的世界观也能激发市场热情，甚至在产品亮相前就吸引关注。创始人主导的销售就是如何将创始人的愿景传递给市场，观察哪些市场群体接受它，又接受其中的哪些部分。这是一个让创始人的愿景与市场现实相契合的过程。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Absolutely. I mean, it is the competitive advantage. I don't think people realize how much of a competitive advantage the founder led sales motion is, for three specific reasons. One is that the founder is the visionary. No one's going to be able to speak to it like they can. No salesperson, really no non-founder. The second is that they are the highest order in the hierarchy of the startup. It's the founder. So the market is excited to talk to a founder because they usually know something that the market doesn't know. And they want to learn and maybe they want to experience something differently. So being able to speak to the person that's running the vision, speak to the person that's crafted the vision. (00:07:50): And then that third piece is that the founder can see something budding in a conversation that a salesperson won't be able to see. And it's those budding moments that's where all the gold lives. And I don't think a lot of founders realize that. Their day one market vision is never the same vision that takes them in a product market fit. And I say that all the time. It's these little budding moments where it's like I was able to get to that budding insight because I went deeper and deeper and deeper and deeper through these calls and these conversations, to fully refine how we want to go out and sell it. And only a founder is going to be able to see those things.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我的意思是，这就是竞争优势。我觉得人们没有意识到创始人主导销售行动能带来多大的竞争优势，原因有三个。首先，创始人是愿景的缔造者。没有人能像创始人那样深入传达愿景——无论是销售人员，还是非创始人高管都做不到。其次，创始人在初创企业中处于最高层级。市场对创始人充满热情，因为他们通常掌握着市场尚未发现的洞察力。人们渴望学习，渴望体验不同的东西。所以能与执行愿景的人交流，与亲手打造愿景的人对话至关重要。（00:07:50）第三点，创始人能在对话中捕捉到销售人员无法察觉的萌芽时刻。而这些萌芽时刻，往往蕴藏着关键的商业价值。我认为很多创始人没有意识到这一点。他们最初的市场愿景与最终实现产品市场匹配的愿景往往大相径庭。我经常强调，正是这些细微的萌芽时刻——比如通过不断深入沟通和对话，最终精确界定销售策略——让创始人得以捕捉到关键洞察。而这些洞察，只有创始人才能敏锐捕捉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this because this connects really well with an episode I just did with the CMO of Wiz. And the founders went through this exactly. They had 10 to 15 conversations a day for weeks, and then they're like realizing people keep telling us they like it, but no one's buying, no one's excited enough to want to actually move forward. And that was only happening because the founders were on these calls.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这一点，因为这和我刚与Wiz首席营销官合作完成的一期节目内容非常契合。创始人们也曾亲身经历过这样的过程。他们连续数周每天进行10到15次沟通，后来却突然意识到，尽管人们不断称赞产品理念，但始终无人购买，更没有人对其充满热情并愿意推进项目。之所以出现这种情况，就是因为创始人亲自参与了这些沟通会议。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, the other thing too is that it becomes a game of telephone. It's like, hey, this salesperson says that no cares about this. What do you think the first thing the founder's going to say is? It's the salesperson. So much easier to say that than, is it me? Is it my vision? So it also kind of brings the accountability closer to the pulse where decisions are made.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说还有一点，就是这变成了一场"传声筒游戏"。比如，销售员说"没人关心这个"，你觉得创始人首先会指责谁？当然是销售员。这样比质疑自己、质疑愿景要容易得多。所以这也让责任追究更贴近决策层面，确保问题能被及时发现和解决。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how similar this is to product building, where there's this idea that a founder top down can tell the team what to build, and it's this very waterfall cycle. When in reality the idea of the product and feature is just like step one, and then there's actually building it, testing it, talking to customers about it, that actually turns that initial seed of an idea to the real thing that people will want.
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，这与产品开发过程极为相似。在传统的瀑布式开发模式中，创始人往往会自上而下地指挥团队开发产品。然而现实中，产品和功能的构思仅仅是第一步。随后，还需要实际开发产品、进行测试，并与客户沟通反馈。正是通过这一系列步骤，原本的创意种子才能最终转化为人们真正需要的实用产品。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny

They just want to build product. They're mostly product people, design people. Sometimes there's founders that are salespeople. Rarely is that the case in my experience. So doing sales is very hard, not something that comes naturally to a lot of people. A lot of people are very afraid of it. So with that, let's get into how to actually get better at the sales process. I think a nice framework for how we can go through this is basically first let's talk about the sales cycle, the steps, the key steps of a sales cycle. And then we'll just go through each step and help people learn some tactics to get through each of those conversations.
turns.zh: 好的。所谓的"进退两难"（Catch 22），虽然我不确定这里是否有这个术语。但核心挑战在于，创始人确实应该负责销售工作。但大多数创始人从未接触过销售，他们只想专注于产品研发。他们大多是产品经理、设计师。当然也有身兼销售职责的创始人，但以我的经验来看，这种情况实属罕见。销售工作确实很困难，对许多人而言并非天生擅长之事。很多人对此心怀恐惧。基于此，让我们深入探讨如何真正提升销售能力。我认为一个有效的框架是，先讲解销售周期及其关键步骤。接下来我们将逐一解析每个步骤，帮助大家掌握应对不同销售场景的策略。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Sounds great.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Yeah. Cool. So what's the simplest way to think about the steps of a sales cycle?
turns.zh: 好的。是啊。不错。那么，思考销售周期各个步骤的最简单方法是什么？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: The traditional sales stages that most CRMs are even set up as is you have your intro call. You have your second call, which sometimes could be the demo depending on the stage of market you're selling to. Then you have your third call, which is going to be more about walking through a proposal, a scope of work, maybe going deeper into the demo to contextualize it to everything you've learned. The fourth call is going to be getting their feedback and kind of co-authoring that scope of work even further. The fifth call is going to be around probably an introduction to procurement. And then selling into procurement in itself, it's its own little sales cycle, but we could talk about that in a sec. And then post-procurement, it's going to be obviously getting that signature and knowing who the actual signatory is. Sometimes it's not even the business unit, it's sometimes legal, CFO, procurement themselves. So just understanding who that is.
turns.zh: 传统的销售流程通常由多个阶段组成，多数CRM系统也会按此结构进行设置。首先是初次拜访。接下来是第二次沟通，视所处市场阶段而定，可能进行产品演示。第三次沟通则侧重于深入解读提案和工作范围，或是结合演示内容，全面呈现已掌握的信息。第四次沟通的重点是获取客户反馈，并进一步完善工作范围。第五次沟通则围绕采购部门展开——这本身就是一个独立的销售周期，不过我们稍后再详细探讨。最后在采购流程完成后，关键在于获取签约，并确认实际签约方身份。有时签约方并非业务部门，而是法务、财务总监或采购部门等相关人员。因此，清晰识别签约方身份至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. So let's walk through each of these steps. So I love that each call has its traditional goal, demo, proposal, then co-authoring, and then procurement, and then post-procurement. I love how consistent everybody is.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。那我们就逐一讲解每个步骤。我很欣赏每个销售电话都遵循传统流程——先设定目标，接着进行产品演示和提案，然后是共同撰写合同，再到采购环节，最后是采购后跟进。大家能如此严谨地执行流程，真是令人赞赏。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, well, it's also, it's interesting because it's also predicated on their buying process as well. So if they're really used to buying, if they're very mature in their buying process, they actually might guide you to what the steps are. But most startups are turning non-consumers into consumers. So that's why this kind of fits well.
turns.zh: 是啊，好吧，这也很有意思，因为这也取决于他们的购买流程。所以如果他们真的习惯购买，购买流程非常成熟，他们或许会指导你了解具体步骤。但大多数初创公司都在致力于将非消费者转化为消费者。因此，这种方法正好很适用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So there's this intra call step. So kind starting about where it begins. I think where a lot of people struggle most is getting anyone to even pay attention. You don't want to talk to them. A billion SaaS tools emailing me constantly about their product. So maybe we start there of just like how do you get someone to even want to talk to you and be open to learning about what you're doing?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以这里有个电话沟通的环节。能不能先讲讲这个环节是从哪儿开始的？我觉得大多数人最头疼的问题是如何让别人愿意搭理你。他们根本不想和你交流。每天都有无数的SaaS工具不断给我发邮件推销他们的产品。所以或许我们可以从这儿入手——如何让别人愿意跟你沟通，愿意了解你正在做的事？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. And this is why that founder led sales piece is so important. One is when it's coming from the founder, it's an entirely different weight. You're like, oh, interesting. This founder is reaching out to me. Okay, I'm going to seek to go a layer deeper, knowing who is sending me this note. The second piece is this is why that novel insight, that technical insight, that business model insight that you've uncovered needs to lead here. People are inspired by a new way of thinking, usually something counterintuitive, something that's really different. I really try and stay away from better, because that's really hard to define, and better means something different to everyone. So if you can focus the messaging in a way that speaks to something that has a bit of shock value, or is counterintuitive, you'll get them to continue reading. So first and foremost, I usually like to open it with, which is why is this relevant for me in my role? (00:13:20): Why are you reaching out to me? So first and foremost is relevancy. I think that matters even more so than personalization right now. I think it's so easy to personalize anything, and it can also come across as really stressed when you're like, hey, I noticed you were on such and such podcast, and that was when they were previously two roles behind. So I always say relevancy. If you can get to relevancy, that's the most important piece. The second most important piece is really getting to that level of differentiation or counterintuitive nature. So say something that would literally make them say what? Or that makes no sense. Maybe not that makes no sense, but what or how could that be? Or I've never thought about it that way. Or I actually don't fully understand what they're saying, but there's something there that's interesting. Get them to pause for a minute. (00:14:13): And the most important piece is getting this done where, if they get it on their mobile phone, which everyone is looking at their mobile phone and on email, they don't have to scroll. So usually three to four sentences max. That also, that's how a founder writes. That's how an executive writes if you're selling top down. But most importantly, leave them wanting more. Don't say everything, don't even talk about the solution. Talk about the problem that you want to solve, and why it needs to be solved or why it's not good enough today. So those are the four main components. Just to reiterate, relevancy, bring some level of counterintuitive or really different approach to the conversation, focusing in on a problem that's predicated to them, and really concise.
turns.zh: 是的。这就是为什么创始人主导的销售策略如此重要。首先，当信息来自创始人时，其分量截然不同。人们会想，哦，有意思。这个创始人主动联系我。好的，我要深入探究一下，看看是谁发来的这封邮件。其次，这就是为什么你发现的新颖见解、技术洞察或商业模式创新需要在此发挥关键作用。人们通常会被新思维方式所启发——尤其是那些反直觉、与众不同的观点。我特别避免用“更好”来形容，因为这个词太难定义了，而且对每个人来说“更好”的标准都不同。所以如果你能将信息聚焦于具有冲击力或反直觉的方面，人们就会继续阅读。因此，首先我通常会开门见山地问：这与我的角色有何关联？（00:13:20）你为什么联系我？所以相关性是重中之重。我认为当下相关性比个性化更重要。个性化任何东西都轻而易举，但有时也会显得过于刻意。比如你说：“嘿，我注意到你参加了某个播客节目，而当时你还处于两个职位之下。”这就显得很刻意。所以我始终强调相关性。若能做到相关性，这才是最重要的。其次，要真正做到差异化或反直觉。比如说些让他们惊呼“什么？！”或“这根本说不通”的话。或许不必直说

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. Is there an example you could share that helps make this even more real? Maybe an email you helped with. And by the way, this is email and LinkedIn, I imagine is where you're communicating mostly?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。你能否分享一个案例，让这件事更具真实感？比如你曾协助处理的某封邮件。顺便问一下，你日常主要通过邮件和领英进行沟通，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: LinkedIn, email, you would be shocked to hear this, but cold calling. I never used to do this. It is one of the most... The interest rates on cold calling are a lot higher than email in many cases.
turns.zh: 领英、邮件，还有——说出来你可能不信——直接上门推销。我以前从不干这种事。但在很多情况下，上门推销的转化率比邮件营销高得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's calling, email, cold email and LinkedIn DMs, is that the three channels generally?
turns.zh: 这么说来，常用的渠道主要有打电话、发邮件、群发邮件以及在领英上发送私信，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep, those are the three, yeah, the main ones.
turns.zh: 是的，就是这三个，对，就是最主要的三个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Yeah. Is there an example? It doesn't have to be word for word which you've done or people done, but just how do you... Yeah.
turns.zh: 酷。是啊。有例子吗？不一定要完全照搬你做过的或者别人做过的，但你能不能讲讲你是怎么做的……嗯。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Actually our first three years were built on cold email before we actually had clients, before we got word of mouth from the founders we worked with, I cold emailed the first 20 customers we had at Jellyfish. And the line I used in there was zero to one sales talent doesn't exist. That's why I want to have a conversation with you. So that was kind of that leading, wait, what? What does that even mean? And what I would do is tie that to them in some respects. If they recently raised the seed or series A, where they are in that journey. But I would lead with that and then tie it into like, hey, I noticed you're looking to target X, Y, and Z based off of what your website. I'd love to have a conversation with you.
turns.zh: 实际上，我们最初的三年都是靠冷邮件开发客户。在获得口碑推荐之前，我们曾与多位创业者合作过项目。当时我在Jellyfish公司时，给前20位客户发送了冷邮件。邮件中我写道："从0到1的销售人才根本不存在"。这句话引起了对方的惊讶，他们回应道："这话什么意思？"于是我会根据他们的具体情况展开对话。比如，如果他们刚完成种子轮或A轮融资，处于项目初期阶段，我会先抛出这个话题，然后顺势提及："我注意到你们的网站重点关注X、Y、Z领域客户，非常希望能与您深入探讨合作机会。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that first piece is the relevance. Here's why this is relevant to you.
turns.zh: 首要一点是相关性。我来解释一下这为何与你息息相关。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. And then I say, our belief at Jellyfish is zero to one sales talent doesn't exist. That's why we built this model.
turns.zh: 是的。然后我要说，在Jellyfish，我们坚信“从零到一的销售人才是不存在的”。这正是我们构建这种模式的原因所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And you kept it really short. So it's relevance, counterintuitive, keep it really short. And then what was the fourth piece?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你把它总结得简洁明了。所以关键点在于相关性、反直觉，还有保持简洁。那第四个要点是什么？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: The fourth piece is just make sure it's concise so that you don't have to scroll on mobile phone.
turns.zh: 最后一点要确保内容简洁明了，这样用户在手机上浏览时就无需过多下滑页面了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While we're on this topic. What's a good conversion rate of these sorts of cold outreaches?
turns.zh: 既然我们正在讨论这个话题，那这些冷销售的转化率一般能达到多少呢？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Conversion rate is interesting. Because everyone's so focused on conversion rate. I get that in the beginning until you have some wins, you have to focus there. But I just want to reverse engineer it backwards a bit. Once you kind of have this, and I'll talk about it in a sec, which is win rate. Win rate is if I got Lenny on a phone call, and he went through the sales process, and I signed him up. And I spoke to 10 Lenny's and only Lenny R was the one that signed. That's one out of 10, that's a 10% win rate. (00:17:23): So if you have a really high win rate, let's say 30 or 40%, you actually don't need as high of a conversion rate on the outbound, because you know if you get someone in the funnel, the throughput is very healthy. If your win rate is really low, you need that conversion rate to be much, much higher, because you need more and more and more at bats. So conversion rate is a funny thing. In the beginning I get it because you don't have a lot of customers going through the pipeline yet. But there's people focus on it in a little bit of a false sense because interest rate truly is also dictated by win rate. So I just want to specify that.
turns.zh: 转化率这个概念挺有意思的。因为大家都太关注转化率了。我理解，在刚起步阶段，直到取得一些成果之前，确实需要把精力集中在这方面。但我只想从反向角度分析一下。等你掌握了某些关键点后（我稍后会详细讲解）——比如胜率。胜率指的是，如果我给莱尼打了一个电话，他完成了整个销售流程，然后我成功签下他。假设我跟了10个莱尼客户，最终只有莱尼R签约了。那么胜率就是1/10，即10%。（00:17:23）所以如果你胜率很高，比如30%或40%，那么你其实不需要太高的外呼转化率，因为你知道只要把客户引入销售漏斗，转化效率就会很高。如果你的胜率很低，那转化率就必须大幅提高，因为你需要更多的尝试机会。转化率这事儿挺微妙的。刚开始我能理解，因为那时你的客户还没大量进入销售流程。但有些人对此的理解有偏差，因为转化率其实也是由胜率决定的。所以我要特别强调这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point.
turns.zh: 这一点说得真在理。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I would say if you're doing a win rate around 15 to 30% and you need to carry, oh I don't know, a million dollar quota. I would say a healthy conversion rate from outbound probably sits around, when it's mature, around five to 7%. Sometimes it could be two to 3%. Sometimes I've seen eight to 15% because it's coming from the founder, and they're solving a really heartfelt problem. So interest rate is also predicated on the problem that the founder has decided they want to solve for, and their insight on that problem. (00:18:51): And everyone wants to keep going back to, well, email rate is really low, email doesn't work anymore. LinkedIn, I'm not getting the connects I want. Yes, you can argue that the game has changed a little bit, but when a problem is truly being felt by the market, people will get on a call. People will respond. And if I can compare two engagements at a time that we're running, I see one where it's a 2% interested rate and then I'm seeing another one that's actually at 12% interested rate. And we're doing nothing different. The only thing that's different is the insight that the founder has on the market, which is a hard pill to swallow. And I know that's hard to hear too.
turns.zh:
我想说，如果你当前的胜率在15%到30%左右，却还得去达成比如100万美元的业绩目标。我认为成熟的外呼业务的健康转化率通常在5%到7%之间，有时可能低至2%到3%。但我也见过转化率高达8%到15%的案例，因为这些项目往往源自创始人亲身经历的痛点，他们正在解决一个真正触动人心的难题。所以转化率的高低很大程度上取决于创始人决定解决的核心问题，以及他们对这个问题的深刻洞察。  

（00:18:51）：很多人总爱抱怨，邮件打开率太低了，邮件营销已经没用了。领英上找不到想要的联系人。没错，你可以说市场环境变了，但当一个问题真正触动市场时，人们就会积极响应。举个例子，我们同时在推进的两个项目，其中一个项目的转化率只有2%，而另一个却达到了12%。但我们两个项目本质上没做任何差异化操作，唯一的区别在于创始人对市场的深刻洞察——这确实让人难以接受，但现实就是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And those are two different companies selling different things?
turns.zh: 还有，那是两家不同的公司，销售不同的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Two different companies selling to two different markets, but they're not fundamentally drastically different markets.
turns.zh: 两家不同的公司面向两个不同的市场销售产品，但这两个市场并非存在根本性的巨大差异。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. But one's basically got more product market fit essentially?
turns.zh: 明白了。但说白了，一个产品是否有市场适配性，本质上主要取决于什么？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's exactly right. So everyone always comes back to we have the sales problem, we have the sales problem, we have an outbound problem. And yes, there could be some technical things going on that you need to look at. Maybe you leveraged clay and you blasted a thousand people and now your domain health has been impacted. But the vast majority of the time, maybe you're just not saying anything interesting at all. Maybe the problem you're looking to solve just isn't widely felt. Maybe the perspective you have needs another level of refinement because you're just not getting those bites.
turns.zh: 没错。人们总是在抱怨"我们有销售难题"、"我们有外呼问题"。当然，技术层面的问题可能也需要排查——比如你用了自动化工具群发邮件，结果域名健康度受损。但绝大多数情况下，根本问题在于你传达的信息不够吸引人。你试图解决的痛点或许并非共性需求，或者你的观点还需要进一步打磨，因为根本没人买账。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like this question you just touched on is something a lot of founders are always wondering, is this product not the thing people want? Is it my sales skills? I guess I imagine this is a very difficult question to answer, especially quickly. I guess is there anything there that's more likely because of this, it means your product isn't something anyone's want, versus you're not doing a good job selling it?
turns.zh: 我觉得你刚刚提到的这个问题，是很多创业者一直困惑的——是不是产品不符合用户需求？还是我的销售技巧不够？我觉得这个问题很难快速给出答案。更深层的疑问是，到底是产品本身没人买，还是你没能有效推广？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Remember that amazing chart you drew where it talked about the length of time it took? I think you picked the top 25 startups.
turns.zh: 还记得你画的那张超棒的图表吗？里面讲的是创业公司所需的筹款时间长度吧？我记得你当时选了前25名的创业公司作为样本分析的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For product market fit timeline [inaudible 00:20:51].
turns.zh: 关于产品市场匹配的时间线 [听不清 00:20:51]。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Product market fit. Yeah, that amazing image that I think has been reshared more times than anything I've ever seen. It's interesting because if you look at, I was looking at this closely the other day. If you look at the top section where the time to product market fit is consolidated, and you go all the way down to the air tables and the figmas, which a long time to get to product market fit. If you think about the earlier ones, which were, it was like GitHub that had product market fit pretty quickly. The SOC 2 compliant company.
turns.zh: 产品市场契合度。没错，就是那张令人惊叹的图片，我觉得它被转发的次数比我见过的任何东西都多。说起来挺有意思的，前几天我仔细研究了这张图。如果你看顶部部分，关于产品市场契合度的时间线被整合得非常清晰，再往下看空白表格和Figma图表，发现有些公司花了很长时间才实现产品市场契合度。再回想早期那些案例，比如GitHub就很快实现了产品市场契合度。而那家符合SOC 2标准的公司，过程则耗时更久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Vanta.
turns.zh: Vanta。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Vanta. There's this thing in my head and I haven't fully validated it but I'm going to share it with you, which is did they start with the market problem first and then build the product? Because they knew who their market was right off the bat. Versus an air table and a figma that I think started with a technical insight and then were trying to find their market.
turns.zh: Vanta。我脑子里有个想法，虽然还没有完全验证过，但还是想和大家分享一下。他们的做法是先明确市场问题，再开发产品吗？因为他们一开始就很清楚目标客户是谁。而像Air Table和Figma这类产品，似乎是先有了技术洞察，然后再去寻找对应的市场用户群体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's absolutely right. Vanta, the way they approached it, Christina, she was searching for a pain. She was obsessed with talking to everybody about a pain that they needed solved, and then she just built it in spreadsheets. So she started with the market very much so.
turns.zh: 我觉得这完全正确。Vanta团队的做法是，先由克里斯蒂娜去寻找用户痛点。她一心想向所有人讲述他们亟待解决的痛点，然后就直接用电子表格把产品功能搭建起来了。所以她一开始就非常注重市场调研。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And I think product market fit when you start with the market first, it's accelerated. But I will say this, I think that it's also capped on the upside. Because you're starting with the market versus the air table and the figma, which started with the technical insight and has uncapped upside. But one is certainly riskier than the other. Starting with a product is a hell of a lot riskier. And this is where I come back to so many people will say, how did you get funding and not know who your market is? And it's like, because if they do find it, that's a really, really, really big win. Versus I think if you start with the market first, you could potentially get a good win but is it more capped?
turns.zh: 另外，我认为如果先从市场入手来验证产品适配性，这样能加速进程。但我也要指出，这种方法在上行空间方面存在局限性。因为你先是针对市场进行验证，而像Air Table和Figma这类产品，则是从技术洞察出发，潜在收益几乎没有上限。但显然，前者比后者风险更高——先做产品再验证市场的策略，失败的概率要大得多。这也让我想起很多人会问：你怎么能在不清楚目标市场的情况下成功融资？对此我只能说，因为如果最终找到了市场，那就是一次巨大的成功。而如果一开始就先验证市场，虽然也可能取得不错的结果，但成功的可能性显然更受限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 真有意思。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I don't know, it's just a thought. I was staring at your grid for so long, I was like, there's something here. And I kept coming back to those were more like I kept breaking it down to market versus product.
turns.zh: 我也不确定，这只是个想法。我盯着你的图表看了好久，突然觉得这里好像有问题。然后我反复思考，最后把它归结为市场与产品之间的关系问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love this. I think there's definitely something there. There's also horizontal versus a very specific problem you're solving.
turns.zh: 是的，我很喜欢这个想法。我觉得这里面确实有潜力。但要注意区分横向应用和你要解决的具体问题。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you mentioned clay and you kind of nerd sniped me there of just what tools do you find useful? And it makes me think about finding leads, which is kind of going backwards through the sales process, but it might be okay, so maybe let's spend time there. Just like what do you recommend to founders to find the good leads? Glengarry Glen Ross good leads.
turns.zh: 好的，你提到了Clay，然后你还故意拿我开玩笑，问我觉得哪些工具比较有用。这让我想到如何寻找潜在客户，虽然这有点倒退于销售流程，但或许也可以考虑一下。那么，你能给创业者们一些建议，如何找到优质的潜在客户吗？《光荣之路》里提到的优质潜在客户就是个很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So I say before you buy any tool, don't even think about tools. I feel like people turn everything into this complicated mess with all of the tools that they start integrating. And then they're engineers, I get it. So now they start to engineer these sales tools together and then they blast their market, and now they have 5,000 notes out in one day and their domain takes a hit. So I think before you even overthink about the tools right now, can you manually find 30 people that you want to spend 15 to 20 minutes writing a rock solid note to? Are there 30 people that you are deeply excited to learn from, that you are willing to invest 15 to 20 minutes to write a really thoughtful note? Let's just start there. So some questions. One, are they even discoverable? How hard is it to find 30 people? (00:24:21): What have you noticed across those 30 people? Are there any interesting insights? Maybe it's the size of the team they work on, maybe it's the industry they're in, maybe it's the length of time they've been in their role, maybe it's their previous roles in their career. Are there some commonalities? There's always some level of a commonality usually in most cases. Okay, so now you're starting to collect some parameters. Just by doing this exercise, you're starting to collect some parameters around who you want to learn from and sell to. Now if you send out those 30 notes and you wrote them specifically, and you spend good quality of time on it. And you've hit them on email, you've hit them on LinkedIn, maybe even tried to call them, maybe you've sent them a Twitter DM, pulled out all the stops. How many people respond? 1, 5, 0? (00:25:15): If it's zero, it begs the question, do you now want to do another 30 in a very similar fashion? Do you want to change the messaging a little bit? Now it forces these natural experiments. Or do you want to maybe go after a different role? So it forces you to answer these questions in a very manual way before you even think about integrating and spending time on tools. And then you get to a point where it's like, okay, now I'm starting to get some learnings and now I've realized, okay, it's this group of people, I've spoken to maybe two or three, now I want to go out and actually build a campaign to now talk to the next 10 to 15 people in that group. Truncate this as much as you can because I think people focus so much on volume in the beginning. (00:26:06): Even if you're selling down market, mid market, enterprise, volume comes once you've identified it and know the parameters. Parameters then allow you to do really strong enrichment with a clay. You now know the types of questions to give it. If you're not asking it the right questions, these enrichment tools, these sales tools will yield nothing. So it all comes back to even before you start your sales call, you need to make sure you're asking the right questions with am I even engaging, or do the people that I want to learn from or sell to, am I even messaging them in the right way? Are they even the right person? And the only way you can do that is by actually truncating these little experiments.
turns.zh: 因此，我想说，在购买任何工具之前，先别急着考虑工具。我觉得人们把一切都搞得太复杂，集成了各种工具。然后他们是工程师，我理解。但现在他们开始把这些销售工具拼凑在一起，然后向市场狂轰滥炸，一天发送5000封邮件，结果域名评分直线下降。所以我觉得，在你过度纠结于工具之前，能不能先手动找到30个人，花15到20分钟给他们写一封高质量的邮件？有没有30个你特别想向他们学习、愿意投入15到20分钟精心构思邮件的人？就从这点开始。接下来几个问题：首先，他们是否容易被发现？找到这30个人有多难？（00:24:21）：在这些30个人中，你发现了什么共性？有没有有趣的洞察？比如他们所在的团队规模、所在行业、任职时长、过往职位经历等。有没有共通点？通常情况下总会有一些共通之处。好的，现在你开始收集一些参数。通过这个练习，你就能初步了解你想向谁学习、向谁销售。现在你发送这30封邮件，精心构思，投入大量心血。通过邮件、领英、甚至可能打电话、发送推特私信，全力以赴。结果有多少人回复？1、5、0？（00:25:15）：如果是0，那就该反思：你还要以类似方式再发30封吗？需要调整信息策略？还是转向不同职位？这样能迫使你以非常手动的方式回答这些问题，再考虑整合工具和投入时间。等你积累了一些经验后，比如和两三个目标人物沟通后，你会发现这批人群值得深入挖掘。尽可能简化这个过程，因为很多人一开始就太关注数量了。（00:26:06）：即使你面对的是低端、中端、企业级市场，数量也是在明确目标群体和参数后才产生的。参数能让你精准使用客户数据挖掘工具。如果提问不当，这些工具就毫无用处。所以关键在于：在开始销售通话前，你要确保问题正确——我是否在吸引目标？我想学习或销售的对象，我是否用正确的方式沟通？他们是否是合适的人选？而这只能通过不断迭代小规模实验来实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how tactical that is. And what I love is even one of your nuances you mentioned is can you even find them? This gives you a signal of how are... You're going to have to have hundreds of these, thousands of these eventually. If 30 is hard or impossible, you're in trouble already.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这种策略性思维了。最让我惊叹的是，你提到的那些细节——比如能否找到它们？这能让你判断一个人的能力如何……最终你得收集成百上千个这样的信息点。如果30个都很难做到，甚至根本不可能，那你就已经陷入困境了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally. And it was funny, I was talking to someone today that said they had a target segment of high net worth individuals that they wanted to go out and serve. I'm like, how do you find those people? I guess when you get to a certain level, your net worth may be public. I don't know. That stuff's very hard to have certain parameters that are undiscoverable. And then if they're undiscoverable and it requires you getting on a call to understand if they are a fit, that does impact conversion rates. Not necessarily in a bad way, but now you need to kind of bring that back into the math equation, which is like, okay, if I speak to 10 people, I know two out of these 10 will be qualified. But I don't know which of those two out of 10. Well, that means you probably need more of those numbers.
turns.zh: 完全正确。说起来挺有意思的，今天我和一个人聊天，他说他们目标客户群体是高净值人士，想去拓展服务对象。我就问："那你怎么找到这些人呢？"他回答："等你达到一定财富水平后，净资产信息可能就会公开了。我也不太清楚。要想设定一些不易被识破的筛选标准，实在太难了。"接着他补充道："即便这些信息难以获取，但如果需要通过电话沟通才能判断对方是否符合条件，这确实会影响转化率。虽然不一定是坏事，但这就需要把这些因素重新纳入计算模型了。比如，我跟10个人沟通，预计其中2人符合条件，但具体是哪两个还不确定。这意味着可能需要扩大潜在客户数量，才能提高成功率。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to quickly recap a few of the key things that I've written down as we're talking. So if you're just trying to figure out who to reach out to, make a list of 30 potential prospects that you think are good fits, that would be excited about what you're building. Spend 15 to 30 minutes writing them each an email. Do these emails have to be really short the way you described previously?
turns.zh: 接下来，我要快速回顾一下我们交谈过程中记下的一些关键要点。假设你正试图确定该联系谁，可以先列出30位潜在合作伙伴，他们要符合你的项目需求，并且对你的创业项目感兴趣。花15到30分钟的时间给每位潜在合作伙伴写一封邮件。这些邮件需要像你之前描述的那样简短吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I would say the shorter the better, but would you respond to that? If you got this email, would you respond it?
turns.zh: 我觉得回复越简洁越好，不过你会回复吗？如果你收到这封邮件，你会回复吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: One of a great little tactical test is on Gmail, you can highlight the message and then have it replay it back to you from an audio perspective.
turns.zh: 一个很棒的小技巧测试可以在Gmail上进行：你可以选中某条消息，然后让系统从音频角度将其重新播放给你听。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You'd be shocked how many notes I've changed when it replays it back and I'm like, oh, that sounds really passive-aggressive.
turns.zh: 你肯定会惊讶，当歌曲重放时，我改了多少个音符。然后我就会想，哦，这听起来真是又委屈又不服气啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. And so you also shared the structure for how to reach out to folks. So let me just share that again. And that applies to this initial email too, but it sounds like as you automate, you want to make it more precise and focused and not... Basically they're not as customized as you start reaching out to more folks.
turns.zh: 很有意思。那么你也分享了如何与他人联系的框架。让我再复述一遍。这同样适用于这封初始邮件。不过听起来当你把流程自动化后，你希望让沟通更精准、更有针对性，而不是……总之，随着联系人数的增加，个性化程度会逐渐降低。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So start with something, here's why this is relevant to you. You're looking for salespeople in this market. Here's something that's unexpected or surprised, like zero to one salespeople don't exist. Keep it short and then I always forget the last one.
turns.zh: 那么就从一些事情说起吧，为什么这跟你息息相关呢？你正在这个市场寻找销售人员。接下来要说一些出乎意料或令人惊讶的事，比如从零到一的销售人员根本不存在。尽量简洁明了，但最后一句我总是会忘掉。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Focus on the problem.
turns.zh: 专注于问题本身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Focus on the problem.
turns.zh: 专注于问题所在。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You don't even need to talk about the solution. That's the big takeaway, which is if you get any sales email, you get what's the primary focus of that email? It's usually like here's what we do. But I bet if someone reached out to you with a novel insight and said, I'm really passionate about solving this problem, if it's something you're focused on, you'd probably reply.
turns.zh: 你甚至不需要谈论解决方案。这才是关键点所在。假如你收到一封销售邮件，首先会关注什么内容？通常都是“我们能提供的服务”。但我敢打赌，如果有人带着新颖的见解主动联系你，说：“我对解决这个问题充满热情，如果这正是你关注的领域，你很可能会回复对方。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If it's a big problem. If it's like, oh yeah, you're so right, I need this.
turns.zh: 要是这真是个大问题的话。要是有人说"哦，对啊，你说得太对了，我就需要这个"之类的话，那可就麻烦了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: The beauty with the American market, and I say this because we do a little bit of work with international startups too, is if something doesn't feel right, people love to complain about it. And it's like use that to your advantage. Get that intel.
turns.zh: 美国市场的魅力所在——我这么说是因为我们也为一些国际初创公司提供过服务——在于，如果某件事感觉不对劲，人们总爱抱怨它。而你完全可以利用这一点来为自己谋利——从中获取宝贵的洞察信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A note that I just looked at, that I wrote down, that I think is very important is avoid using "this is better" as your pitch.
turns.zh: 我刚刚看了一张笔记，上面写着一条我认为非常重要的建议——避免用“这个更好”来作为你的推销说辞。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, yep.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Different. Here's something shocking about what we're doing. Here's something that'll surprise you.
turns.zh: 不同之处在于……以下是我们正在做的一件令人震惊的事。接下来要告诉你们的，会让你们大吃一惊的。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, or counterintuitive. Exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，或者说这有点违背直觉。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Counterintuitive.
turns.zh: 真令人难以置信。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. I spoke to a good friend that leads procurement at a massive organization. And he said to me, he goes, "One of the worst things someone can say to me is we're better than X product. Then I ask them to define that. And then I ask them, okay, how do we measure that? And then I say, okay, should we give this company another year to give them this feedback before we make this huge transition and disrupt momentum?" Yeah, better is a dangerous place.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很有意思。我和一位在大型机构负责采购的朋友聊过。他跟我说：“别人对我说‘我们的产品比X产品更出色’，这简直是最糟糕的评价了。然后我会反问他们：‘你能具体说明‘更出色’体现在哪些方面吗？’接着我会追问：‘那我们该如何衡量这种‘更出色’呢？’最后，再反问一句：‘在我们做出重大调整、打破现有发展势头之前，是否应该再给这家公司一年时间，让他们先完善产品，再给出最终反馈呢？’没错，追求‘更出色’往往会陷入危险的境地。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I invest in a bunch of startups and I find it's impossible to get anyone to care if things are good enough with what they got today. I'm happy not using the best possible product if my life is okay. And I have so many other things I got to do, I'll just deal with this good enough solution for now.
turns.zh: 我投资了不少初创公司，但发现即便现有产品已经足够好，也很难让人们真正在意是否能做得更好。只要生活还过得去，我宁愿不去追求最完美的产品。况且我还有太多其他事务要处理，暂时先用这个差强人意的解决方案应付一下也无妨。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing. So we talked about how to figure out who to go after, how to pitch them to get them to want to talk. The next step I imagine is you're on the phone with them trying to convince them to actually care. What do you do there? How do you get them to engage further?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我们之前讨论了如何确定目标客户，以及如何向他们推销产品让他们愿意沟通。接下来，我想你可能会和他们通电话，努力说服他们真正感兴趣。在这个环节你会怎么做？如何让他们进一步参与对话？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: One is you need to be vulnerable. You're an early stage startup, okay. The market, we're at a point now where the market is smart. I always assume that the buyer I'm speaking to is highly educated and knows way more than I do. So just have that perception because what I've learned is a lot of the market will play dumb, and you can get yourself caught pretty quickly. So when you speak to them, I would be very open and honest with where you are. Hey, I'm an early stage startup. We are deeply passionate about solving this specific problem. We have a lot to learn. Here's how we are thinking about it from a problem priority perspective. Can we gain your insight into how this problem is manifesting on your side? And then let them open up. Now you have them one, talking about the problem. Now you're getting the intel about their perception of the problem, and is it even a problem? When you say you're early stage and there's still a lot to be done, it is easier to be honest. (00:32:20): If you tell them you have a fully baked, ready to go product, they're not going to give you honest feedback. It's very hard to say to a founder and look them in the eyes and say, hey, we built this product, can I show you what it is? You're just going to get someone that's going to say, oh, this is great, this is wonderful. But when you're vulnerable and when you tell them it's not fully built yet, even if it is, you will get more raw and honest feedback. Because it is easier to tell someone, hey, before you make this mistake, I actually don't care about that. If you've already built it, they're not going to give you that feedback. So the further you suggest you are, you're actually going to hamstring a lot of the intel, hamstring yourself on gaining a lot of the intel. So that's one counterintuitive thing that I think a lot of founders don't realize.
turns.zh: 其中之一就是你需要保持坦诚。你们是一家处于早期阶段的初创公司，对吧？当下市场已经变得越来越精明。我总是假设与我沟通的买家受过高等教育，比我懂得多得多。所以你要保持这种认知，因为我的经验是，许多市场参与者会装糊涂，你很容易被套路。所以当你与他们交流时，我建议你要坦诚相待。比如说：“我们是一家处于早期阶段的初创公司。我们对解决这个特定问题充满热情，但仍有许多需要学习的地方。以下是我们从问题优先级角度出发的思考：能否请您谈谈这个问题在贵公司是如何呈现的？” 然后让他们畅谈问题。这样一来，你就能了解他们对问题的看法——甚至确认这是否真的是一个问题。当你坦言公司尚处早期阶段、仍有大量工作要做时，反而更容易获得真诚反馈。（00:32:20）如果你告诉他们产品已经完全成型、随时可以上线，他们就不会给出真实反馈。很难直视创始人说：“我们开发了这款产品，能否给您演示一下？” 对方只会附和：“太棒了，太棒了。” 但当你保持脆弱态度，坦言产品尚未完全成型（即便实际上已经完成）时，就能获得更真实、更诚恳的反馈。因为人们更容易说：

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: She's awesome.
turns.zh: 她太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And her last book, it actually has the opposite advice, but I think I know why, which is she focuses on later stage companies and her advice is the buyer. She has this really interesting insight that it's harder to buy software now than to sell it, because there's so much to consider and your job is on the line if you make a mistake. It's easier just to be like, forget it, I'm just going to go with what we have today. I don't want to put my ass on the line for buying this new thing that someone's trying. And so her advice is you actually have to educate the buyer on the market and here's what's happening. Here's where things are going, and here's why I think this is the future. But I think again, I think that's focusing on later stage stuff.
turns.zh: 太神奇了。她上一本书里的建议恰恰相反，但我觉得我明白原因——她主要研究的是后期阶段的公司，而她的建议针对的是买方。她提出了一个很有意思的观点：如今购买软件比销售软件更难，因为需要考虑的因素太多，一旦出错，自己的职业生涯就悬于一线。相反，人们更倾向于想"算了吧，还是用现有的产品吧"，不愿冒险去尝试新事物。因此，她的建议是，你必须向买方普及市场动态，告诉他们行业发展趋势，以及为什么你认为这项技术是未来的趋势。不过，我还是觉得这种策略主要适用于后期阶段的公司。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: A hundred percent. And you raised such a good point, Lenny, which is late stage sales and early stage sales are very, very different. And I think that's where a lot of early stage founders get tripped up as they're taking late stage sales advice, usually coming from an investor. Or they've maybe hired a salesperson that's focused on more mature sales. But I think she's spot on. Buying is just as hard, if not harder, than selling right now. Because who wants to make a mistake and also who wants to go through switching costs? Oh, it's so painful.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。莱尼，你提出了一个非常好的观点——晚期阶段的销售和早期阶段的销售有着天壤之别。我认为这正是许多早期创业者容易陷入的误区，他们往往会采纳来自投资者的晚期销售策略建议，或者聘请专注于成熟市场销售的销售人员。但我完全认同你的观点：当下买入产品和服务的难度丝毫不亚于销售过程本身。毕竟，谁愿意犯错呢？更何况还要承受转换成本的煎熬？这实在是太令人头疼了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think the other really important point here that you're making is that part of this initial sales experience of founder led sales is not sell as much as you can. It's to learn what people want. And so I love that you're sharing here's how to get the best possible feedback, not necessarily close the most deals.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为你提到的另一个重要观点是，在创始人主导销售的初期阶段，关键不在于尽可能多地推销产品，而在于了解客户的需求。所以我很欣赏你分享的这些方法——它们旨在获取最有价值的反馈，而不一定是为了达成尽可能多的交易。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally. And founder led sales is not about revenue on day one. It is about learning as fast as humanly possible to get to that pulse, so that you can earn the right to sell. There's this concept that I talk about, which is you're going out to run sales to collect the research, which is what founder led sales is. And then you have sales for revenue, which is that post founder led sales stage.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。创始人主导的销售模式关键不在于第一天的营收，而是要尽可能快速地掌握市场脉搏，进而赢得销售资格。我常提到的理念是，创始人外出开展销售工作主要是为了收集市场洞察，这正是创始人主导销售的核心要义。而后续的营收阶段则需要正式的销售团队来实现目标，这才是创始人主导销售阶段过渡后的自然发展阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And your milestone that you suggested of how far to take founder led sales, you said around a million ARR, right?
turns.zh: 还有你提到的关于创始人主导销售的里程碑，你说要达到大约100万美元的年度经常性收入（ARR），对吧？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. I think it's about, some people say 500, some people say a million. I think if you get to 500K really, really fast, then I think absolutely you can move out of it. If you get to 500K really, really, really slow, you might not want to get out of it right away. You haven't reached that velocity point yet.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这得看情况，有人说50万，有人说100万。我觉得如果你能很快积累到50万，那你肯定能摆脱这种状态。但如果你积累速度非常慢，可能就不想急着脱身了。因为你还没达到那个关键的增长速度呢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I have a post that we'll link to that has actually numbers and when all these big startups move from founder led sales. It's in that same series about product market fit. There's two stories this makes me think of I'll share real quick. One is Sprig. They shared a story of first round capital at their first round and their partner there is just like, we will not let you hire a salesperson until you hit a million ARR. We're going to help you. We're going to have salespeople helping you through it, but we're not going to let you hire someone. And he was really happy about that. The other is Zip, which just raised a $2.3 billion valuation, a procurement company that I was lucky to be an investor in. And their first founder led sales motion was they just reached out on LinkedIn to heads of procurement, and just leaned into what you're saving more, which is we just want your advice on this product that we're building. Just tell us what problems you have. It was very advice oriented versus we want to sell you this thing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我有一篇文章会附上链接，里面有具体数据，讲的是当这些大型初创公司从创始人主导销售转向专业销售团队时的情况。这篇文章属于同一个系列，主题是产品市场契合度。我马上能想到两个案例，跟大家快速分享一下。第一个是Sprig。他们在首轮融资时分享了一个故事，投资方当时提出条件：在达到年化经常性收入（ARR）100万美元之前，公司不能招聘销售人员。投资方承诺会派销售团队协助，但坚决反对直接招聘销售人员。Sprig的创始人对此深感欣慰。另一个案例是Zip，这家刚以23亿美元估值融资的采购公司，我有幸成为其投资者。他们首轮由创始人主导销售的策略是，直接在领英上联系采购部门负责人，突出产品能为客户节省成本的价值主张。他们更关注客户需求，说：“我们正在开发这款产品，非常希望听取您的意见。请告诉我们您目前面临的痛点。”整个销售策略更偏向提供专业建议，而非强行推销产品。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, no, absolutely. I have this theory that maybe you shouldn't hire any salespeople until series A, right? Because seed is all about experimentation and proving out that experiment, and then obviously series A is about exploiting that learning. But I see so many people, I mean hiring for early stage sales is the odds are actually more against you than trying to get your next round of funding. Because it's truly, truly such a counterintuitive stage.
turns.zh: 是啊，不，绝对没错。我有个观点——或许在A轮融资之前，你根本不该招聘任何销售人员，对吧？因为种子轮阶段主要在于试验和验证这个试验的可行性，而A轮融资阶段显然就是要利用这些经验来获取更大收益。但我见过太多例子，说实话，早期阶段招聘销售人员的成功概率，远比你争取下一轮融资要低得多。因为这个阶段的挑战实在是太反直觉了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Okay, so I kind of took us on a whole tangent. You were sharing advice on how to get someone excited. You were going to go to the next tip and I took us off course.
turns.zh: 真有意思。好吧，我有点跑题了。你之前是在分享如何让别人兴奋起来的建议。首先，在与潜在客户和ABC公司沟通时，要坦诚且真诚地谈论自己的项目阶段。告诉他们你还处于早期阶段，正在打造这个产品，对这个问题充满热情。向他们说明我们的工作重点、优先考虑的问题，以及我们目前的专注方向，同时征求他们的反馈意见。不错。你本来要讲下一条建议的，结果被我带偏了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Testing the questions to ask. Where is that aha unlock for you? But more importantly, where's that aha moment unlocked for them? This is a really powerful thing, which is like, so tell me how this looks in your head? How are you seeing this? And they're like, I don't know if I can see it. And I'm like, great, we'll show you that. Great insight to know by the way. Or so I think this is how, I guess this is how it would work. Walk me through what's living in your head right now. You pick up on so much and then all of a sudden they're like, wait a second, we've tried solving for this and it's still not solved for. Or you know what? We hired someone last year to manage this. Great understanding. Is it being measured? Is it being managed and have they tried to solve for it? The leading indicators that you're onto something here.
turns.zh: 测试要问的问题。那个"啊哈时刻"对你是从哪里来的？但更重要的是，对他们而言，那个"啊哈时刻"又从何而来？因为当他们开始在脑海中构思时——这正是产品尚未成型且未向他们展示时的妙处——他们此刻正在脑海中进行可视化构想。这真是件极其强大的事情。比如，你可以问："这在你脑海中呈现的是怎样的画面？你具体是如何理解的？"他们可能会回答："我不确定自己能否想象出来。" 你接着说："太好了，我这就展示给你看。顺便说一句，这真是深刻的洞察力。" 或者你可以说："我猜这大概是这样运作的。" 再引导他们："请跟我讲讲你此刻脑海中浮现的画面。" 你会捕捉到大量关键信息，突然间他们会说："等等，我们之前尝试过解决这个问题，但还是没能成功。" 或者："你知道吗？我们去年就为此聘请了专人负责。" 这些都是你判断自己找到了关键问题的指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this thread because this is what everyone's always like, how do I know if I product market fit? There's these signals that you're talking about of signs that there's something here. Like a big enough pain point where they're excited to basically they want to pay for it, they will pay to solve a problem. So maybe just again, say the things you notice that are signs like, okay, you have something here.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这个话题，因为这正是大家经常遇到的困惑：如何判断产品是否符合市场需求？你提到的那些信号，确实能预示着项目存在潜在价值。比如，用户面临的痛点足够强烈，他们愿意为此付费，愿意花钱来解决问题。或许你可以再列举一些能说明项目有前景的关键信号，让大家更直观地感受到其价值所在。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So I think the first is it has to be a growing and widening problem. No one's going to spend time fixing a pretty fixed problem, because it's not necessarily really a priority anymore. It's maybe a pain in the butt, but it's not a priority if it's not growing or widening. So gate check one is like, what is the implication? Are you measuring? Are you managing this problem today? Yes or no? If they don't know, great to know. If they said no, okay, move on to the next. That's pretty powerful. No, we're not measuring or managing this. Okay, there's probably not much there. If it is being measured or managed, then the next question you want to get into is how have you tried to solve for it? Is it through that head count that you just hired? Is it through another tool? Is it just still an open gap because nothing exists yet to solve it? Just understand their maturity around how they've tried to plug it. These are all that make the secret moments in intel to close that gap.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为首先，这个问题必须是一个不断恶化且日益严重的挑战。没人会花时间去解决一个相对稳定的问题，因为它已不再被视为当务之急。它或许令人头疼，但若问题未呈扩散或加剧趋势，就谈不上优先级。所以，首个筛选问题是——你是否有相关衡量指标？当下是否在积极管理这个问题？答案若为否，自然无需多言；若答是，那接下来就该深入探讨：你们是如何尝试解决的？是通过新招募的团队成员？还是借助其他工具？抑或仍存在空白待填补？通过这些问题，我们能精准把握客户在缩小知识鸿沟方面的成熟度差异，这些关键洞察正是弥合知识鸿沟的核心密码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. And essentially it's showing you that there's a pain here that they're paying attention to and are trying to solve.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这本质上是在向你表明，他们注意到了这里存在的痛点，并正在努力解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And what you're psychologically doing is now you're flipping them into a buyer where they're like, wait a second, hold on. I need to bring on so-and-so on the next call, they also think that this is not good enough.
turns.zh: 你们现在在心理上做的是，把他们转化成买家。他们会想，等等，等等。下次通话时我需要把某某也接进来，而且他们还会觉得这还不够好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's funny because that's exactly what Wiz noticed, is they moved from people being like, oh, this is cool. I like it, I like it. To, okay, I'm going to pull in this person. I'm going to pull in this person to talk about it and make sure we're... And they were pulling in other people exactly as you described it, because they wanted to move forward on this thing.
turns.zh: 真有意思，因为Wiz也注意到了这一点——他们从最初的"哇，这真酷，我喜欢它"，转变为"好的，我要拉这个人进来聊聊，确保我们……"。正如你所描述的，他们确实在不断拉拢其他人，因为他们想推进这件事。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Absolutely. And that's when you know there's some momentum behind it, which is when they're bringing in other colleagues. Whether it be the potential users, if you're reaching out to the executive, or the users like, hey, I actually want to bring my boss on to the next call.
turns.zh: 没错。这时候你就能知道背后有股推动力了，因为他们会拉来其他同事。无论是潜在用户、向高管汇报，还是让用户主动邀请老板加入下次通话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good sign. Cool. Anything else along these lines of how to get someone excited slash understand if there's going to be pull there?
turns.zh: 好兆头。太棒了。还有其他能激发对方兴趣、让他们明白有合作可能的技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I guess the one thing is please, please, please do not ask questions like what keeps you up at night? If you had a magic wand, what are your pain points today? I can guarantee you that answer changes every single day.
turns.zh: 我觉得最重要的是千万别问"什么让你夜不能寐？"或者"如果你有魔法棒，现在最大的痛点是什么？"之类的问题。我保证这些答案每天都在变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's super interesting. Is there any tip for how to end one of these calls, as someone that's never done sales is like-
turns.zh: 太有意思了。对于结束这类通话，有什么建议吗？比如——

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 有啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Pull up calendars. Look at calendars. Who else should be invited? It's just a natural evolution to ending the call.
turns.zh: 调出日历看看。还能邀请谁？这自然而然就是结束通话的流程。

turns.en: Great. So that's in 30 minutes though, right?
turns.zh: 好的。那30分钟后见，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And if they say, ah, I'll email you.
turns.zh: 要是他们说"我会发邮件给你"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could say.
turns.zh: 我可以回一句。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's also kind of a leading indicator. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这也是个预警信号。对。

turns.en: So do you recommend not getting off the call, trying to avoid that, or is it just-
turns.zh: 那你建议别结束通话？还是说——
