turns.en: If they won't give you time on the calendar, you could say, listen, great. Feel free to email me. Maybe they're just being honest and they don't have their calendar available, but nine times out of 10, it's usually I don't have the heart to tell you I'm not interested.
turns.zh: 如果他们不给你日程安排时间，你可以说"好的，没关系。随时发邮件给我。"可能他们只是实话实说日程太满，但十有八九是因为他们没兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's hard. It's hard to tell people you're not interested. Very cool. Okay. This is amazing. Okay, so the next step, if I remember correctly, is kind of co-authoring and co...
turns.zh: 是啊，真难。很难告诉别人你没兴趣。太棒了。好的。这太棒了。好的，下一步如果我没记错的话，应该是共同创作和合作……

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。说说这个吧。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: In the early, early days, one of the biggest ways you can get folks excited is it feels like it's going to be built specifically for them. The power of specificity, the power of being extremely focused. With that, you can literally turn a customer into a guide by asking them to co-author the scope. The scope of work. The co-authorship piece is important for two reasons. It helps you understand where they're on their biomaturity. Let me explain. If they do not have an existing process or strategy to solve X problem, they can't buy a technology yet, which means you need to sell them. And this is why I go back to you need to sell them some form of a service, right? Why? You want to be the one in there educating. You also want to get the logo. You also want to show the revenue. While it's not recurring revenue, it still shows intent. (00:44:13): And I think that that's really important. Every founder I speak to is like, well, my investor really doesn't want service-based revenue. That's fine. But then you can also tell your investor, great, should I wait 18 months to when they're ready to buy a solution, and be the one that's not the one selling them because someone else educated them? These are all of the implications of waiting. So yes, is service-based revenue great? No, we all know why it's not great. But it's great in the sense that it shows intent. It's great in the sense that you can call them a customer. It's great in the sense that now you can use their logo. And it's great in the sense because you are getting paid to educate them. You are getting paid to help them design their process. This is where all the power lives. And this is why so many AI startups a year and two years ago were going in on services contracts, because they wanted to set the mindset with the buyer around what this would look like.
turns.zh:
在早期阶段，让人们兴奋不已的最有效方法之一，就是让他们感觉产品是专为他们量身打造的。这种针对性的力量，以及高度聚焦的能力至关重要。通过邀请客户共同参与项目规划（即范围界定），您能真正将客户转化为产品导向者。这种合作模式的重要性有两个方面：一是能帮助您了解客户在生物成熟度方面的现状；二是能让客户深度参与项目规划，形成共创成果。

共创环节之所以重要，有两个核心原因：首先，它能让您精准把握客户的需求点。如果客户尚未建立解决某个问题的流程或策略体系，他们就无法直接购买相关技术，这意味着您需要主动为他们销售解决方案。这也正是为何我反复强调——您必须为客户提供某种形式的服务支持。为什么？因为您需要承担教育客户的角色，同时争取客户的认可，展示业务成果。即便这些收入并非循环性收入，但至少能证明客户的意向。

（00:44:13）我认为这一点至关重要。许多创业者都会抱怨：投资人不认可服务型收入模式。这没关系。但您可以反问投资人：那我是否要等18个月，等他们准备好购买解决方案时，再把项目交给其他公司？这种等待的代价不言自明。诚然，服务型收入模式并非完美，但它能证明客户的意向，让您获得客户的认可，使用客户的品牌标识，同时通过教育客户、协助他们设计流程来创造价值。这些都是其核心价值所在。这也是为何两年前许多AI初创公司纷纷签约服务合同的原因——因为他们希望从一开始就让客户树立正确的思维模式，明确合作的边界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you recommend to time box contain the services piece? Because I know a lot of companies-
turns.zh: 您是否有时间管理技巧来控制服务部分的进度？因为我知道很多公司——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes, such a great point, Lenny. You absolutely need to time box this. I would time box it as 90 days and then what you can say in the next 90 days, we'll scope where we are and what you need. Scoping out more than 90 days, listen, so much is going to change. You might also not want to do it anymore, so you don't want to lock yourself up. So I would look at 90 day increments. A specific example. We had a founder that my colleague was working with, and they were selling a very specific technology to a non-traditional... Sorry, a very traditional industry. I don't want to be two bleeding with what it is, but a very traditional industry that's not used to working with startups, or necessarily plugging in a new technology right away. And they were very honest. They said, listen, we haven't changed vendors or partners in over five or six years. (00:46:04): I actually don't even know how we would do that today. Could you come in and explain to us, understanding where our workflow is and how we would integrate this, before we even consider the technology? Which we did. We got paid a nominal amount, but we're now a customer and now we get to set the stage for how they think about this. And then they won the technology contract. But everyone is so focused on selling the technology really, really, really quickly. That works in markets that know how to buy that technology, have a process in place, have a strategy in place, have an implementation team in place. (00:46:40): If it's a new technology like AI right now, they need a strategy and process like who's the human in the loop? Is it them or is it you? How do we measure success? What does success look like? What risks should we be aware of? Our legal team's not even aware of all these risks. You want to be careful because legal can immediately, and procurement, can shut these things down if it seems too novel, where it's foreign versus they're so used to buying services, especially at market. It's their largest budget line item.
turns.zh: 是的，伦尼，你说得太对了。你绝对需要把这件事分阶段规划。我建议把时间周期定为90天，然后在接下来的90天里，你可以先评估现状和需求。规划时间超过90天的话，要知道未来会有太多变数，你甚至可能不想继续推进了。所以我建议以90天为一个阶段。举个具体例子吧。我们曾和一位创始人合作，他的产品是向一个非常传统的行业（我不想透露具体行业名称）销售一项特定技术。这家公司对新技术、新合作模式都非常陌生，他们坦诚地说："我们五六年都没换过供应商或合作伙伴了。现在连怎么引入新技术都不知道。"（00:46:04）我们先是免费做了咨询，帮助他们理解现有工作流程和整合技术的流程。最后他们赢得了技术合同。但大多数人一心想尽快把技术卖出去。这种模式只适用于那些熟悉购买流程、制定了策略、组建了实施团队的市场。比如当下热门的AI技术，要考虑的风险包括："人工干预环节在哪里？是他们还是我们负责？如何衡量成功？成功标准是什么？"我们的法律团队甚至都未能预见到所有这些风险。大家要谨慎处理，因为法律部门和采购部门可能会因技术过于新奇而叫停项目，毕竟这类技术对他们来说是陌生的，而他们更习惯于购买现成的服务，尤其是标准化市场中的服务——毕竟这是他们最大的预算支出项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's interesting because most founders are very afraid of moving into services. I hadn't heard this advice before.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，因为大多数创始人都非常抗拒向服务转型。我之前从未听过这种建议。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Probably going to get slapped for saying all this stuff, by the way.
turns.zh: 说这些话估计会被批评的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, so along those lines, what percentage of companies that you've worked with or see do that or have to do that step?
turns.zh: 所以按照这个思路，你合作过或见过的公司中，多少比例需要先提供某种服务才能销售技术？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: This is going to be a shocking step. So I would 40 to 50% have to sell some form of service before they can sell a technology.
turns.zh: 这会是个令人震惊的步骤。所以我认为40%到50%的B2B SaaS公司在卖技术前都必须先提供某种服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Of B2B SaaS company?
turns.zh: 哇，针对B2B SaaS公司吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: A B2B SaaS. And this, again, this is specifically more top-down sales. But yeah, because the user and the buyer are different, which means there's user value, there's buyer value, there's all different players, there's procurement you have to go through. But yeah.
turns.zh: 就是B2B SaaS。再说一次，这更多是自上而下的销售模式。但没错，因为用户和购买者不同，这意味着有用户价值、购买者价值，参与方各不相同，还有采购流程需要突破。不过确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to make it even clearer, what's an example of a service that you've seen company offer in a step?
turns.zh: 再具体点，你见过哪些公司提供的服务作为过渡阶段？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So I've seen, hey, can you come in and actually help me pitch this, design a custom pitch to my boss as to why we should do this today? And we literally got paid to build a sales pitch.
turns.zh: 比如，我见过这样的例子："你能不能来帮我设计一个定制化的推介方案，向老板说明为什么我们今天就该推行这个技术？"结果我们直接收钱帮他们设计了销售方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's not necessarily providing a service. It could be just helping them sell this.
turns.zh: 所以不一定是提供服务，可能只是帮助他们销售。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. It could be helping them sell in a way that makes you... You need to get a lot more context on their business. It can also be, hey, we haven't actually thought about a process for how we can actually deploy something like this. We're currently using this technology, which we want to change from. You've kind of hit this at the right time. How would we implement or how is it best to integrate with this tool? Can we get both of you guys in a room to map this out?
turns.zh: 是的。他们可能是想通过某种方式帮助你销售产品，让你……你需要更深入地了解他们的业务。这也可能是，他们还没有真正思考过如何部署这样的产品。我们目前正在使用这项技术，但想对其进行改进。你来得正是时候。我们该如何实施，或者如何与这款工具进行最佳集成？能否把你们俩召集到一起，共同规划方案？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it's like consultants almost, like coming in to help you solve this problem.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以这就像是顾问服务，帮助他们解决问题。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's a great point. It's consulting them towards the acquisition of the product. It's not consulting as one-off consulting.
turns.zh: 说得太好了。这是在为他们的产品采购提供咨询服务，而不是一次性咨询。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And they know that obviously you're biased, but they also want the problem solved. And they're like, great, you're going to help us solve this problem, because it's on my plate and I need your help convincing leadership that this is-
turns.zh: 懂了。他们知道你可能有偏见，但还是希望问题能得到解决。他们会说，太好了，由你来帮忙说服领导层，因为这事由我负责，我需要你的帮助。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And I need to craft the storyline as to why we need to do it anyway, so I will pay you to do it, but here's the format it needs to be in.
turns.zh: 我需要构思一个说服方案，说明为什么我们必须这么做。然后我会付钱让你来做，但格式必须符合要求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. Wow. Okay. Anything else along those lines?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。哇。好的。还有其他类似的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And then of course, if you're in a position to actually sell the technology, because the market is able to acquire and adopt it and not have to create a new strategy or process, then obviously sell the technology. You don't need to be selling services.
turns.zh: 当然，如果你有机会实际销售这项技术，因为市场能够接受并采用它，而无需制定新的策略或流程，那显然就该卖技术了。你不需要卖服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back real quick. The previous call, I wrote this note down as you were talking. You recommended not doing a demo and just talking about it broadly.
turns.zh: 我想再快速回顾一下。上次通话时，我在你发言时记下了笔记。你建议不要做演示，只需广泛讨论。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that your advice there?
turns.zh: 这是你的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: On the first call. Yeah. On the first call, my fundamental belief is that the demo is a bit of the only carry you control in the sales process, right? Once they see it, it's kind of like pitching an investor. Once they take a look under the hood, that dreaminess in their eyes, they're like, oh, I saw it. So leave them wanting more. And the demo is that, leave them wanting more. Even when you do a demo, don't demo everything. Leave it for a second call. Let them invest a lot of time in you. Again, if it's qualified. Preface that, if it's qualified. But everyone races through the sales process like let's do a demo call as quickly as humanly possible. (00:50:20): Yes, that is important down market. That is important if you're selling a $3,000 tool, you absolutely want to be demoing as fast as humanly possible because it's a high-volume game. Upmarket, when you're talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars, you want to slow that down as fast as possible. Because you want to, one, make sure all of the right people are in the room. As soon as there's one lead on this, and if it requires other people involved, it doesn't feel like anyone else's baby. So you want it to make it feel like the group's baby versus this one individual's baby because it's very quick. Someone can easily say, I'd rather use this tool. And then there's this stalemate of nothing happens.
turns.zh: 在第一次通话中。是的。在第一次通话中，我的基本观点是，演示是销售过程中你唯一能控制的环节，对吧？一旦他们看到演示，就有点像向投资者推销。一旦他们深入了解，你眼中那种梦想般的光芒，他们会说，哦，我看到了。所以要让他们意犹未尽。演示就是要让他们意犹未尽。即使做演示，也别全展示出来。留到第二次通话。让他们在你身上投入大量时间。前提是他们有意向。但很多人在销售过程中急于求成，比如尽快完成演示通话。这很重要。（00:50:20）：是的，这在低端市场很重要。如果你卖的是3000美元的工具，你肯定想尽快完成演示，因为这是一个高容量游戏。高端市场，当你谈论数十万美元时，你就想尽可能放慢速度。因为你需要确保所有合适的人都在场。一旦有一个人对此感兴趣，如果还需要其他人参与，就会觉得这不是别人的事。所以你要让它成为整个团队的事，而不是某个人的事，因为速度太快了。有人可能会说，我宁愿用这个工具。然后就会陷入僵局，什么都进展不了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to maybe reiterate, so far we've talked about figure out who to talk to, pitching them on talking to you, then having that first conversation. Maybe there's another conversation in there to get them excited. And then there's just getting them past the finish line, keeping everyone aligned. Is that roughly the next step or how should we think about this?
turns.zh: 可能需要再强调一下，到目前为止，我们讨论了如何确定要与谁沟通，向他们推销与你交流的机会，然后进行首次对话。或许还需要再进行一次对话来激发他们的兴趣。接下来就是如何让他们最终达成合作，确保各方目标一致。这大致是下一步的流程，还是说我们应该从另一个角度来思考这个问题？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, so if you are selling upmarket and you now need to go to procurement, who is the group involved in the bot. They're the professional buyers. Procurement is a very interesting function. They are very smart, very, very smart. They do this for a living. They are professional buyers. So there's a couple things that you need to be aware of. You need to sell them as well. You need to really make this sound... Don't over complicate it. Don't add in jargon. Make it feel like, okay, I can wrap my head around this. The second piece is it's got to feel different from anything else out there. Because the professional buyer, it's much easier to say, wait a second, we have these 17 other preferred vendors that do similar ish work. Why don't you just go use one of them? Because, oh, by the time this gets through procurement, it could be another three to four months. (00:52:05): I've seen deals die on the vine because procurement actually suggested they go use another vendor in the system, that this buyer wasn't even aware of, because they didn't differentiate. It didn't feel different. It just felt slightly better. That's how it was positioned. The third piece is when you get to procurement, you're going to have to do all the work. Make their job easy. You are probably a very small piece into the very large deals that a lot of these people buy. So you can get easily sidelined just because you're just a small buy. So do the work for them. Literally say, I want to make this as easy as possible for you. Give me the forms that you need to fill out. I'll fill them out for you, and you can do it yourself. You can edit them. Do the lift for them. If you don't, it's so easy for it to just go there and die. (00:52:55): Another piece that's important with procurement is explaining exactly what you do and don't do. Because if you say you do a bunch of things and they can't really place you, they're going to send you to the kitchen sink of contracting an MSA, which is going to ask you for $5 million in an insurance policy and all sorts of other things. And the ability to look at your book at any point in time. And the reason they did that is because they can't classify you. So the easiest thing to do is classify you as high risk. So make it easy for them, make it simplified. You can also truncate your contracts, meaning let's say IT is maybe, and you want to ask this, how long does it take to get through IT due diligence? They might say, oh, it's a 90-day backup, it's a 60-day backup, it's a 30-day backup. (00:53:43): There's no backup. If there's a backup, you also don't want it to die and you want it to give an incentive. So this is when you want to truncate contracts to a technology contract and a service contract. Service contract allows you to onboard them, get them prepped, come in and educate all of the users about what they're about to go through. So that then there's an incentive to get that technology piece through. There's all these little things to think about, and I think everyone... Getting to procurement is also creative. And knowing who you're dealing with and how to make their job as easy as humanly possible. Because what you said and what April said is spot on, which is buying is just as hard as selling.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以如果你在销售高端产品，现在需要去采购部门，那些参与采购的人是谁呢？他们是专业的买家。采购部门是一个非常有趣的职能。他们非常聪明，极其聪明。他们以此为生，是专业买家。所以有几件事你需要注意。你得把产品卖给他们。必须让他们觉得这东西确实有价值。别把事情搞得太复杂，别加进那些行话。要让他们觉得，嗯，我能理解这个。第二点是，你的产品得和市场上其他同类产品有所不同。因为采购人员会想，等等，我们系统里还有17个类似业务的首选供应商，你为什么不去用他们呢？因为一旦采购部门接手这个项目，可能又要拖三四个月。（00:52:05）我见过很多交易因为采购部门建议客户去用系统里的其他供应商而夭折，因为采购人员根本不了解这些供应商。他们没法区分差异，觉得产品只是稍微好一点。这就是他们给出的理由。第三点是，当你接触到采购部门时，你必须把所有工作都做好。让他们的工作变得简单。你可能只是大单子中的一小部分，而很多采购人员买的都是大单子。所以你很容易被忽视掉。那么就为他们省点事吧。比如，直接说，我想尽可能让你们的工作更轻松。给我需要填写的表格，我来填，你们自己再编辑。为他们减轻负担。如果你不这么做，交易很可能就黄了。（00:52:55）还有一点很重要，就是要准确说明你的业务范围和不涉及的业务。因为如果你说你能做很多事，而他们又没法给你分类，就会把你归到高风险类别。所以最好让他们分类时简单明了。你也可以精简合同。比如，IT部门可能需要90天备份，60天备份，30天备份。但其实根本没备份。如果有备份，你也不想让它拖太久，还要给出激励措施。这时候你就需要把合同精简成技术合同和服务合同。服务合同能让你先培训用户，让他们做好准备，进来后再给所有用户讲解即将开展的工作。这样就能激励他们推进技术部分了。还有很多细节需要考虑，我觉得每个人……接触采购部门也是需要创意的。要了解对方的需求，尽可能让他们的工作简单易行。因为你和April说得都很到位，就是采购和销售一样难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As I'm hearing you describe this, I feel like we might be discouraging people from selling because this feels very not fun. All these steps, all these procurement work, anything you can say to get people to feel like, okay, this is worth it?
turns.zh: 听你这么描述，我觉得我们可能在劝退销售人员，因为这听起来一点都不容易。这么多步骤，采购工作这么繁琐，你能不能给点建议，让人们觉得，嗯，这值得努力？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes, I can get people very excited by this. Once you are in, you are in. Once you are in, you are now a preferred vendor. You now have the ability to cross over into other business units. You are now the reason that, hey, if your competitor comes in, well, you got there first. So what do you think procurement's going to say? This is why it's so important to get into the enterprise as fast as humanly possible. While it's a headache to get through, if you project manage it, you'll be good. If you make an accountability, just like if you were to go through fundraising. If you are a part of a team that had to raise money, it's no different. There's always some level of due diligence. There's always you doing more of the work than them. That's just enterprise sales. But if you prove value, your hundred thousand dollars deal could be $500,000 next year. Your $500,000 deal could be a million dollars the following year. (00:55:36): This is where stuff begins to compound, and this is where your growth journey really gets accelerated. So the beauty with enterprise is once you're in, you're in. You beat out your competitor for a short period of time. There is a little bit of a moat there, but it's not forever. You all have intel that no one else will have. Meaning you're a part of the conversations, you have the badge, you can join the meetings, you can ask for introductions. They'll do it. It doesn't feel like sales anymore. You're now a partner. This is why it's so powerful to get into the enterprise because there's so many compounding effects. If you put the effort in on the sales side, the return is insane.
turns.zh: 是的，我能让人们对此兴奋不已。一旦你成功进入，就意味着你正式成为首选供应商。此时你将有机会拓展到其他业务部门。现在你就是那个关键因素——如果竞争对手来挑战你，你已经抢先一步占据了先机。那么你觉得采购部门会作何反应？这就是为什么尽快打入企业市场至关重要。虽然过程会令人头疼，但只要你能有效规划项目，一切都会顺利。如果你能像筹集资金时那样建立责任机制，那就没问题了。如果你所在的团队需要筹集资金，道理是一样的。总会有一定程度的尽职调查，总会是你比对方付出更多努力。这就是企业销售的常态。但只要你能证明价值，今年10万美元的合同明年可能涨到50万美元，次年又可能突破100万美元。（00:55:36）这就是效益递增的阶段，也是你的增长之路真正加速的时刻。企业销售的魅力在于，一旦你成功进入，就能在短期内击败竞争对手。虽然存在一定的护城河，但并非永久不变。你掌握着别人无法获取的信息——你能参与高层对话、佩戴专属徽章、参加重要会议、主动寻求资源对接。他们会配合你。这不再是传统意义上的销售，而是合作共赢。正因如此，成功打入企业市场意义非凡，带来的复合效应极其显著。只要你在销售端投入足够精力，回报将远超想象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was awesome. Nailed it. I'm excited. Just for folks that are listening, just to calibrate what size of company you're talking about selling to here, what's the size of the advice you've been sharing so far? Roughly?
turns.zh: 太棒了。讲得太到位了。我很激动。给正在收听的听众说明一下：你所提到的销售对象公司规模有多大？到目前为止，你分享的建议主要针对哪类公司？大致说一下。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So I've been talking a lot about enterprise sales, which is I would say anywhere north of 500 to a thousand employees. Just mental model. I'm talking about enterprise sales specifically because there's so much nuance involved in it, because the user and the buyer are very different, right? As you go down market, let's talk about small business for a second. The user and the buyer are the same person. There's no procurement. If they like what you've built, it's pretty straightforward process. In the mid-market, mid-market is a funky place because you either are anchoring towards the lower end of mid-market, which is more upper end of small business, or you're anchoring towards lower end enterprise. Those are two very different divides. So mid-market, just if you're talking about lower end enterprise, again, this is all relative. If you're talking about lower end small business, again, your user and the buyer probably are the same person, which makes sales a lot more streamlined. (00:57:31): But churn. Small business, challenge with small business is the churn. If they get pissed off, if they don't feel like it's good enough, they are gone faster than you don't even realize. And they might even tell you. They'll just cancel. And we always see this on Twitter. They'll call American Express and say, cancel these charges. I don't want to talk to these people anymore. They're just more irrational because sometimes maybe it's their money if they're a small business. So small business in mid-market, while sales is a bit faster, you really got to be on the product market fit side, worried about churn.
turns.zh:
到目前为止，我一直在谈论企业销售业务，我认为这类业务的客户规模通常在500至1000名员工以上。这只是一个思维模型。我之所以特别关注企业销售，是因为其中涉及诸多微妙之处——毕竟用户和采购方往往是两个不同的角色，对吧？当我们深入细分市场时，比如中小型企业领域，用户和采购方通常是同一人，根本无需经过繁琐的采购流程。如果他们认可你的产品，整个销售过程就会变得非常简单直接。中端市场则是个复杂的领域，因为你要么定位在中端市场的低端（即小型企业的上限），要么定位在中端市场的低端（即大型企业的下限）。这两者有着截然不同的市场分野。所以在中端市场，如果你针对的是低端企业客户（这其实也是相对的），那么用户和采购方很可能是同一人，这使得销售过程更加顺畅。

（00:57:31）：但客户流失问题。中小型企业的挑战在于客户流失。一旦他们感到不满，或者认为产品不够好，就会迅速离开，甚至可能直接取消订阅。我们在推特上经常看到这样的情况：用户打电话给美国运通，要求取消收费，说“我不想再和这些人合作了”。中小型企业客户往往更情绪化，因为他们可能是在用自己的钱投资业务。所以在中端市场做中小型企业销售，虽然进展更快，但你必须确保产品与市场高度契合，同时还要时刻关注客户流失问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they also go out of business at a higher rate.
turns.zh: 而且他们的倒闭率也更高。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so you have that kind of churn.
turns.zh: 所以就会出现这种客户流失的情况。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: A churn piece too. Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 客户流失也是个大问题啊。是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. What comes next? So we're kind of in procurement at this point.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来是什么呢？现在我们要谈采购流程了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Okay, so now we're at signature, right?
turns.zh: 好的，那现在我们要谈签约流程了，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Okay. So as you enter procurement, okay, you want to know before you get to the next stage, who is signing this deal? Here are some examples of signers I've seen. Chief financial officer, chief legal officer, the business unit head themselves, the head of procurement. You want to know who that person is so that you can literally say to the head of procurement, hey, listen, I want to make sure this person has everything they need when they review this, to know what they're signing. Who is it and how can I give you a few bullets to share that you can maybe respond to, that we get tight so that they know exactly what they're looking at? (00:58:59): This was two or three years ago, I was involved in getting a deal over procurement that was just truly, it was a pharmaceutical company and it was very, very long process. And we got to the finish line and the CFO was the signature. And this is when I made the mistake. CFO responds back to the procurement lead who sent it to the business unit, who sent it to me and was like, what am I signing? I don't actually understand what these people are doing and why are we doing this? (00:59:32): So then she quickly said to me, hey, listen, we need to defend this. Can you put together some bullets? And I'm like, well, what kind of bullets do I need? What does this person care about? And again, it created so much anxiety and now I'm back in the bottom of the queue. Probably he or she's looking at the things that come in in an order of priority. So now I've elongated this by another month simply because I didn't plan. So this is just to say I'm learning from my own mistake of know who the signature is, because if they don't know what they're looking at, they're going to kick it out and you're going to lose your queue spot.
turns.zh: 好的。所以当你进入采购流程时，好的，在进入下一阶段之前，你需要知道谁会签署这份合同？以下是我见过的一些签署人例子：首席财务官、首席法务官、业务部门负责人，还有采购负责人本身。你需要知道这个人是谁，这样你就能直接对采购负责人说：嘿，听着，我想确保在他们审阅合同时，能让他们清楚自己签署的内容是谁签署的。那是谁呢？我该如何给你一些要点供你分享，让他们清楚自己在看什么？（00:58:59）：这是两三年前的事了。我参与过一个制药公司的采购项目，整个过程非常漫长。我们终于到了收尾阶段，签署人是首席财务官。这时候我犯了个错误。首席财务官回复发送合同给业务部门的采购负责人，而业务部门又把合同发给我，她问：我要签什么？我根本不明白这些人在做什么，为什么要这么做？（00:59:32）：于是她很快对我说：嘿，听着，我们需要为这个合同辩护。你能整理一些要点吗？我问：那我需要什么样的要点？这个人关心什么？结果这又引发了大量焦虑，现在我又排到队尾了。很可能他或她会按优先顺序处理收到的材料。所以我又把整个流程拖延了一个月，就因为我没有提前做好规划。所以我要说，我从自己的错误中吸取教训，知道签署人是谁很重要，因为如果他们不明白自己在看什么，就会把合同退回，你就会失去排队的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many ways to fail. And this was you selling Jellyfish or this was you working with a company?
turns.zh: 失败的方式太多了。这是你卖Jellyfish还是和其他公司合作？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: This was me helping [inaudible 01:00:15].
turns.zh: 这是我在帮助[音频缺失01:15]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Okay. Anything else in that step that might be helpful to folks?
turns.zh: 天哪。好的。在这一步中还有什么对大家有帮助的吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes. One thing to caveat is you do not get paid until you are approved by finance, and procurement has a signature on the contract. Meaning don't start any work. Or if you do start work, know that there is no payment. The business unit can't just pay you. It's paid through a purchase order, which is paid through by finance.
turns.zh: 是的。需要注意的一点是，在财务部门批准合同并签署之前，你是拿不到钱的。这意味着不要开始任何工作。即使你已经开始工作了，也要知道没有支付款项。业务部门不能直接付款。款项是通过采购订单支付的，而采购订单的款项是由财务部门支付的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So don't rely on that money unless it's finally, unless the signature's on the paper. Quick tangent, thoughts on discounting at any parts of the journey?
turns.zh: 所以除非合同最终签署，否则不要指望能拿到钱。顺便说一句，在整个流程的任何阶段考虑折扣问题吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If there is a reason as to why. So discounting just to get the deal over the line, you're negotiating with yourself. Unless they ask for it and then ask them to defend it. Certain segments, like small business, you should leave a little bit of room for buffer because sometimes that's their own money. It's like their own small business. Mid-market and enterprise, there's got to be a reason why and ask them. Be like, hey, so if I give you a 30% discount, can I remove 30% of the value? You can kind of play it a little bit like that. I don't recommend it, but that's kind of what they're saying. But discounting is great if they're doing something for you far and beyond. For example, if they're a design partner, if they're going to be a reference for two years, if they're going to give you something far beyond just using the technology, then yeah, I think a discount is a good reason to give back to somebody that's giving to you, but not as a strategy to get a deal done.
turns.zh: 好的，如果有这样一个原因的话。那么为了达成交易而随意打折，就是在跟自己谈判。除非对方主动提出要求，然后让他们给出合理解释。对于某些客户群体，比如小型企业，你应该留出一定的谈判空间，因为有时那是他们自己的资金。就像他们经营自己的小企业一样。对于中端市场和大型企业客户，必须要问清楚原因。比如，你可以这样说："如果我给你30%的折扣，能否相应地降低30%的价值？"这样处理比较灵活。虽然我不建议这样做，但这确实是他们的策略。不过，如果对方为你提供了超出预期的价值，比如作为设计合作伙伴、愿意作为客户案例展示两年、提供远超技术应用本身的增值服务等，那么给予折扣以回馈合作伙伴是合理的，但不应将其作为达成交易的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Is there anything beyond this step of getting the signature? Are we done?
turns.zh: 好的，除了签约这个步骤，还有其他需要注意的吗？我们已经完成了吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. I hope you celebrate because-
turns.zh: 是的。希望你能好好庆祝一下，因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. You got a signature from this whole process.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。整个流程下来，客户终于签约了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Hopefully I'm not making this sound too daunting. I'm just really trying to lay out all the mistakes I've made.
turns.zh: 是的。希望我没有把这事说得太复杂。我只是想把自己犯过的错误都分享出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, no, this is exactly what people need. This is amazing. And your pep talk was really helpful too. Along the way. What's the general timeline for sales process like this in your experience, with these 500 plus ice companies?
turns.zh: 是的，没错，这正是人们需要的。太棒了。你的激励话语也非常有帮助。一路走来，在你看来，像这样的销售流程，针对500多家冰雪公司，大致的时间线是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So there's three things that dictate sales cycle. One is how well are you project managing it? For example, I'll say, let's have our second or third call in two weeks. Two weeks? Do a week. Why are you elongating this? Keep your calls as tight as possible because that shortens your sales cycle. The second is just how complex the organization is. If you're dealing with a highly regulated industry, just know it's going to take a bit longer, sometimes 20 to 30% longer. So a highly regulated industry, nine to 12 months on conservative, on the conservative side. Again, it's tricky because is there a budget line item dictated towards it yet, or are you creating budget? How painful is the problem? And how senior have you gone? If you're talking to the SVP or chief of whatever, they're pretty good at about being able to navigate the traps. (01:03:28): If you're dealing with a director or mid-level person, they maybe have not purchased something before and just make some internal mistakes. I always say it can range anywhere. I've seen enterprise deals close in 90 days, believe it or not. Rare, but I've seen it. I've also seen enterprise deals typically take anywhere between six and 12 months. Really important but. Enterprises know that the process and the length to get the deal done is what costs more than the technology itself. Meaning the effort it takes to get through their system. That's why they're willing to spend so much. Sometimes that's actually more expensive than the technology itself. So don't negotiate with yourself, understand the value you're delivering, but don't be crazy. I've seen people try and go in with a million dollar deal as a seed stage startup. Oh, interesting thing. So interesting tactic. I've seen contracts in the enterprise that state that the deal cannot exceed more than 20% of the existing revenue. (01:04:39): So there are these things just to be aware of. In most cases, you can ask them be like, is that a hard line? Is that hard, hard line? Or how negotiable is that? Sometimes it's negotiable. Sometimes it's like, no, this is a hard rule. But then it seems silly because you take a hundred thousand dollar deal and bring it down to 20,000. It's just be careful that you're stripping some of the value out. But I kid you not. I've seen an enterprise deal go from, it lands at 60 and it turns into 280,000 in four months. So again, I want to encourage, yes, this is a lot of work, but the payoff is exponential.
turns.zh:
影响销售周期的因素主要有三个。首先是项目管理能力。如果你说"我们两周后再进行第二次或第三次沟通"，客户可能会反问"两周？那就一周吧"。这时候你要反问自己：为什么要拖延？尽可能缩短沟通周期才能加速销售进程。其次是客户企业的复杂程度。如果面对高度监管的行业，周期会明显延长——通常需要多出20%至30%的时间。因此针对这类行业，保守估计周期为9至12个月。再者，要考虑客户是否已有预算线项或正在制定预算，以及问题的紧迫性如何。若对方是SVP级别高管，他们通常能有效破解障碍；但若只是中层管理者，可能缺乏经验，容易犯错。

（01:03:28）：有时企业级交易能在90天内完成，但这种情况极为罕见。通常周期在6至12个月之间。需要注意的是，企业更关注技术之外的系统集成成本，这也是他们愿意支付高价的原因。切勿自我设限，要明确自身价值，但也要保持理性。曾见过初创公司试图与SVP级别高管谈论百万美元级别的大单。还有企业合同中规定交易金额不得超过现有收入的20%，这类条款通常可以协商，但也有严格执行的案例。例如，原本60万美元的合同四个月内飙升至28万美元，足见其中的博弈空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a good ACV to start with if you're trying to sell to enterprise, to make it all worth it for your startup?
turns.zh: 如果要向企业客户销售产品，初始ACV（年度合同价值）应设定为多少才能让初创公司真正受益？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I would say anywhere between 50 to 200K depending on the business unit you're selling to. That's kind of like sweet spot. They're used to something in that realm.
turns.zh: 取决于目标业务部门。通常5万至20万美元是合理区间，符合他们的预算预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is a startup selling [inaudible 01:05:38].
turns.zh: （此处可能存在音频缺失，01:05:38后未能录音）

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Early stage startup, like founder led, early stage.
turns.zh: 初创公司，尤其是创始人主导的早期阶段公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Initial contract. Wow.
turns.zh: 初始合同。哇哦。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep. Initial contract. I would say, okay, probably caters more towards like 50 to 100K. But I've seen people sell to... Again, it's how big is the problem? Who are you selling it to? Is it the SVP that you started with and they've got a large budget, and it's a pretty healthy business unit? Or are you selling to a director?
turns.zh: 是的。初始合同。我认为50至10万美元比较合适。但也有例外，比如问题有多严重？客户是谁？是SVP级别高管吗？他们是否有充足预算且业务部门健康？还是只是普通主管？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you're not able to sell your product at that price? What's your advice to teams?
turns.zh: 如果你无法以那个价格销售你的产品？你对团队有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If you are a startup, I always ask the founder, did you build this for the enterprise and is that the model you want to play? Or did you build this for small business? Small business is a marketing game. Marketing intensive activity, right? It's high velocity, high volume, lots of dials. It's a very different game than enterprise. So which game do you want to play? Let's just start there. Which game is more attractive to the founder. Or who is more exciting to serve? What's the storyline you want to tell investors? That plays a lot of it into it too. And do you have an enterprise product? Are you solving an enterprise problem or do you think you're solving an enterprise problem but you're not sure yet?
turns.zh: 如果你是一家初创公司，我总是会问创始人，你们是为企业打造这款产品的，还是想走这条路线？或者是为小型企业打造的？小型企业是一场营销游戏，是高强度营销活动，对吧？节奏快、交易量大、需要频繁调整。这和面向企业的模式截然不同。所以你想走哪条路线？我们就从这儿开始。哪条路线对创始人更有吸引力？或者说，谁更值得为之服务？你想向投资者讲述怎样的故事？这也很重要。还有，你们有面向企业的产品吗？你们是在解决企业问题，还是自以为在解决企业问题但其实还不确定？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And your point is also mid-market is it's rarely to be successful.
turns.zh: 你的观点也是，中间市场很少能成功。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's hard to start there because you're straddling two very different go-to-markets, right? One that's of high value, one that's of high volume. And also mid-market companies, this is where a lot of people don't... If it requires heavy integration, they don't have those resources. That's usually outsourced to an Accenture or some of these consulting firms, and now you're having to rely on third parties to be involved. It gets messy.
turns.zh: 从这里入手很难，因为你要横跨两个截然不同的市场准入策略，对吧？一个是高价值的，一个是高交易量的。而且，中间市场公司往往没有足够资源进行深度集成，这类需求通常外包给埃森哲等咨询公司，而现在你不得不依赖第三方参与，事情就变得一团糟了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is fascinating. I have a list of questions from the audience that you pulled from Twitter. You asked on Twitter what questions to ask you as you're coming on here. So there's one that's very related to this, which is someone said, if you're still very early in pre-product market fit, but get initial validation from both small to medium businesses and enterprise, how do you decide which one to focus on? Is there a counter argument against starting or SMB going up market over time like most companies do?
turns.zh: 这很引人入胜。我从Twitter上收集了观众的问题清单。你在Twitter上问大家来这儿提问时想问什么问题。其中一个问题和这个很相关，有人说：如果你还处于产品市场适配的早期阶段，但已经获得了中小型企业和企业的初步验证，该如何决定专注哪一个？有没有反对从中小型企业起步、然后随着时间推移向企业升级的观点？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I've seen companies successfully do in both of those motions. Truthfully. We know all of those. We know people that started small business and worked their way up into enterprise and were successful. We've seen people be really successful by starting at the enterprise, like a Wiz. That's more of an internal question, which is like, who did you build this for? Where's the problem most felt and which go-to-market game do you want to play?
turns.zh: 我见过很多公司在这两个方向上都成功了。说实话，我们对这些案例都很熟悉。我们认识很多从中小型企业起步、后来成功进入企业市场的创业者。我们也见过像Wiz这样从企业内部起步、后来走向成功的案例。这更多的是一个内部问题：你为谁打造了这款产品？哪个市场的问题最明显？你想玩哪种市场准入策略？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think that latter part is so important. It sounds like why should it be what I want? It's like what's going to make a big business? But I think people forget, this is going to be your life for 10 years. Do you want to be selling to enterprises and building all the enterprise features? Would you prefer to build for small companies? Pros and cons to both but it's important to think about the life you're creating for yourself and your team.
turns.zh: 我认为后半部分非常重要。听起来这像是为什么要按我的想法来？但人们往往忽视了，这将决定你未来十年的生活。是想专注于企业销售，打造所有企业级功能？还是更愿意为小公司打造产品？两者都有利弊，但重要的是要考虑你和团队将创造怎样的生活。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: A hundred percent. And I built my career in enterprise sales, upper-end mid-market enterprise sales, and yeah, that's just the game I know the best.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我在企业销售领域打拼了一辈子，尤其是高端中端市场企业销售领域，这才是我最熟悉的领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's also an important part of it. Just to double down on that is like what do you have experience doing? Not like...
turns.zh: 是的，这也是很重要的一点。再强调一下，就是你有什么经验？不是说……

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Where's the opportunity? Okay. Another question that I love is, and we touched on this initially, but I think it's good to come back to this. Someone said, customers are fascinated with what we're offering from the initial calls, but responsive momentum is too slow from their end. Would be great to know how to fix this.
turns.zh: 是啊，那机会在哪里呢？好的。还有一个我很喜欢的问题，我们之前也提到过，但再回顾一下也很好。有人说，客户对我们最初的沟通很感兴趣，但他们那边的响应速度太慢了。想知道怎么解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, it's tough because unless you're in the weeds to understand why. I'll give you a few examples that it could be. Did you speak to a buyer who now is trying to sell this up to their boss, and it's just getting sidelined and they don't know the executive value? They've just been selling the buyer value the whole time. That's one reason things can slow down. Another reason things can slow down is you haven't really framed the problem well and they don't understand the full implications of why they need to solve it. So it's kind of just sitting there a little bit. The third is they've just been really nice and it's not going to go anywhere.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很难，除非你能深入理解原因。我举几个可能的原因。可能是你跟的买家现在正试图向上汇报，但被搁置了，因为他们不了解这项技术的价值。他们一直只在强调买家的需求。这是原因之一。其次，你可能没有很好地界定问题，所以客户不明白为什么需要解决它。所以事情就卡住了。第三，他们可能太客气了，但实际上没啥进展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess that that's usually the latter. Was that true or it's kind of all over the place?
turns.zh: 我猜后者更常见。是这样吗？还是说情况很复杂？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's so hard to give a founder hard feedback. Because they've just dedicated their life to this thing. Who wants to be the bearer of bad news? And sometimes you just need to let the actions speak louder than words.
turns.zh: 给创始人反馈真的很难，因为他们把整个生命都投入到这件事里了。谁愿意当那个坏消息的传递者呢？有时候你只能让行动来说话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've talked about all these steps. I'm curious, when you come to a founder or your team, where do you find the most on lock often? Which of the steps of the sales process do you find the biggest opportunity to improve conversion in sales?
turns.zh: 我们已经讨论了所有这些步骤。我很好奇，当你面对创始人或团队时，你最常发现哪里存在问题？在销售过程中，哪个步骤最能提升转化率？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's qualification. Qualification because if you spend your time on the wrong leads, that equates to a zero. So if you don't get that first level right, let me put it this way, everyone that I know says they have a bottom of funnel problem. It's never a bottom of funnel problem. It's a top of funnel problem. I've actually never seen a bottom of funnel sales problem. It's always qualification, which is a symptom of not reaching out to the right person, not having the right messaging, not solving the right problem, or not being different enough.
turns.zh: 是资格筛选环节。原因是如果你把时间花在错误的线索上，结果就是零回报。所以如果第一步没做好，我这么说吧，我认识的每个人都说他们有“漏斗底部的问题”。但这根本不是漏斗底部的问题，而是漏斗顶部的问题。我从没见过真正的“漏斗底部”销售问题。问题总是出在资格筛选上，而资格筛选的核心在于：没有联系到正确的人、没有传达正确的信息、没有解决正确的问题，或者没有足够的差异化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. So basically the biggest pitfall people fall into, in your experience, is they're just talking to the wrong people, wasting their time?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。所以根据你的经验，人们最常犯的错误就是找错了人，浪费了时间？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Talking to the wrong people or using the wrong message or...
turns.zh: 是的。找错了人，或者用了错误的信息……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Pitching them something they can't actually deliver.
turns.zh: 推销给他们一些他们根本无法实现的东西。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Here's the other thing too. Sales is supposed to feel fun for the buyer. They should be like, this feels fun. This person's invigorating. They're going to change my world. They're going to make me see things differently. They're going to get me promoted. They're going to help me increase my influence internally. And so many salespeople are so boring. How many times have you got off a call and you're like, I can't wait to get off this call? And founders too, just like all of a sudden their passion, they go like stone cold face. And it's like bring the passion. Bring the energy. That is felt by the market. Remember, some of these people are in boring jobs. Give them an outlet.
turns.zh: 是的。还有一点。销售本该让买家感觉有趣。他们应该觉得这很有趣。这个人很活力四射。他会改变我的世界。他会让我看到事物不同的视角。他会让我升职。他会帮助我在公司内部提升影响力。然而很多销售人员太无趣了。有多少次你挂掉电话后会想，真希望这通电话快点结束？还有创始人也是，突然间他们的激情就消失了，就像石头一样冷酷。就应该把激情带进来。注入活力。这是市场能感受到的。记住，有些人工作太无聊了。给他们一个出口吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those lines, I think a lot of people are just not... Like me included. I feel weird doing sales. It's a weird experience trying to convince someone to buy something. Is there any advice you could share to get someone over that hump?
turns.zh: 这么说来，很多人都不太愿意做销售……包括我自己。我觉得做销售挺奇怪的，试图说服别人买东西真是一种奇特的体验。有什么建议能帮人克服这个心理障碍吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If you have built something that you believe in. Very hard to sell something you don't believe in. I think everyone agrees that. If you've built something you believe in and they have a problem, that's a beautiful thing. Truthfully, that's what makes the world go around, is I have a solution to your problem. Now you just need make sure that the problem, you just need to be honest, that the problem they have, your solution truly can solve for. And you're not short selling just to get a logo and a deal over the line, and see them churn in six months or nine months or three months. That what you are selling is truly going to solve their problem. And be honest about it. I can't tell you enough when I tell someone, listen, I don't think I'm the right fit for you. They try and sell you on them. (01:12:58): They're like, well, wait a second. Hold on. What if we did this, this, and this? And it's like, no, no, no. Here's what we're great at. And then they can say, well, I also need that too. And all of a sudden, this level of trust comes out. And trust is the number one currency in sales. If you are a trusted salesperson, people will recommend you all day and every day. If you're a trusted founder, your market will continually send you leads and word of mouth. So don't try and sell something just to prove to investors you sold something, because it'll be quickly seen on the other side when they churn.
turns.zh: 如果你打造了一个自己深信不疑的产品。很难推销自己不相信的东西。我想大家都认同这一点。如果你打造了一个自己深信不疑的产品，而客户又遇到了问题，那真是再好不过了。说实话，这才是世界运转的法则——我能为你的问题提供解决方案。现在你只需要确保客户的问题真实存在，诚实地告诉他们，你的解决方案确实能解决他们的问题。而不是为了拿下一个客户或一份合同就降低标准，最后客户在六个月、九个月或三个月后就流失了。你推销的东西必须真正能解决他们的难题，并且要诚实面对现实。当我对某人说"听着，我觉得我不适合你"时，再多的技巧也无济于事。他们会试图说服你："等等，等等，如果我们这样做、那样做，问题就能解决了。" 而我会说："不，不，不。这才是我们的专长。" 然后他们会说："嗯，我还需要那个功能。" 突然之间，信任感就产生了。而信任才是销售的首要货币。如果你是一位值得信赖的销售人员，人们会源源不断地为你推荐客户；如果你是一位值得信赖的创始人，你的市场也会不断为你输送潜在客户和口碑推荐。所以别为了向投资者证明自己做成了交易而去推销产品，因为对方很快就能看穿你的虚伪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, Jen, so I'm going to cut the lightning round. I know you also have to run and do real work. So let me give you a chance just to talk about what you do, how you help companies in case folks can find value in working with you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，Jen，我要结束这个快速提问环节了。我知道你还要去忙正事了。所以我给你个机会，谈谈你的业务，讲讲你如何帮助其他公司吧，如果有人能从中找到合作价值的话。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Deeply passionate about sales, as I'm sure you can tell. We specifically help founders through this pain. Navigating enterprise sales, mid-market sales, and really trying to crack that first million of ARR. Or sometimes even that first 500K of ARR if they move fast enough. And it is really hard. It's counterintuitive to what most people think, but it can be really, really fun when we show you the way.
turns.zh: 我对销售充满热情，这一点你肯定能感觉到。我们专门帮助创始人克服销售难题。应对企业销售、中端市场销售，真正突破首个百万ARR关卡。有时甚至能快速突破50万ARR关卡。这确实很难。这与大多数人的直觉相反，但当我们为他们指明方向时，过程会变得非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you described to me how it works, and I think it's important to clarify this. You basically embed with the team and help them do this.
turns.zh: 你之前给我描述过你们的运作方式，我觉得有必要澄清一下。你们基本上是融入创始人团队，协助他们推进销售工作。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes. So I fundamentally do not believe in outsourcing the heartbeat of the organization, which is sales. So what we do is we embed alongside the founder and drive a lot of the execution, but make sure that they are the tip of the spear engaging directly with their market, and learning directly from the market's mouth, not playing this game of telephone.
turns.zh: 是的。我根本不认同将销售这种组织的核心职能外包出去。所以我们的做法是与创始人深度合作，推动大部分执行工作，但确保他们始终是直接与市场对接的先锋力量，直接从市场获取反馈，而不是玩那种传声筒游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And I mentioned this when we were chatting, but I think of it again, is when I was interviewing all these companies about how they started selling early on. One of the interesting threads that I heard again and again, is how many of them hired a coach or a consultant as a founder to help them learn to do sales. And that's essentially what you do. And I didn't even know a service like this existed, so this is super cool. It'll point people to what you do. I also have to ask you, the question I ask everyone at the end is just, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我之前和大家聊天时提过这事，但现在再想想，我在采访那些早期就开始销售的公司时，发现一个有趣的共性——许多创始人都会聘请销售教练或顾问来帮助自己学习销售技巧。而这正是你所做的。我甚至不知道有这样的服务存在，真是太棒了。这能让人们更清楚你的业务方向。我还想问你一个问题，我在每期节目结尾都会问所有嘉宾：听众如何能为你带来帮助？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Help each other out. I think so many people have helped me in my career, and in this journey, that the pay it forward model that exists in the technology space is so beautiful. So just don't let that die.
turns.zh: 互相帮助吧。我职业生涯中得到了很多人的帮助，在这段旅程里，科技行业互助的精神真是太美好了。所以别让这种精神消亡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Well, Jen, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。珍，非常感谢你今天做客节目。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Lenny, this was awesome. Thank you so much for having me.
turns.zh: 伦尼，你今天的分享太精彩了。非常感谢邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So awesome. So excited for folks to hear it. I've learned a ton. Okay, I'll let you go. Bye everyone. (01:15:41): Thank you so much for listening. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at Lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我学到了很多。好的，我先挂电话了。大家再见。（01:15:41）：非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期节目有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅。也欢迎给我们评分或留下评论，这对其他听众寻找播客会有很大帮助。您可以访问Lennyspodcast.com查看往期节目或了解更多信息。下一期节目见。
